AKS + Terraform Hands-on Guide for AWS Engineers

Engineers who know EKS and VPC build a production-grade AKS cluster with Terraform, following Azure best practices. Every piece of code comes from real files that pass terraform validate and terraform test.

Terraform 1.16.5azurerm 5.9.0AzAPI 2.13.0AKS (Kubernetes) 1.36Azure CLI 2.86+As of 2026-10-13
Start with the AWS ↔ Azure comparisonJump into the labs
Overview

A hands-on guide for engineers who know EKS, VPC, and IAM to build a production-grade AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service) cluster with Terraform, following Azure best practices. Each lab is an independent Terraform stack, and every piece of code in the docs comes from real files that pass terraform fmt, validate, and test.

Read it online: English HTML guide · Korean HTML guide

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stacks Prerequisite
About 4–6 hours in total About $2–2.5 per hour while stacks 03–05 are running terraform/* 01. Prerequisites
❗Important

On top of static validation (terraform fmt, validate, and terraform test with a mock provider), the code in this guide was run end to end, Lab 01–11 from scratch, in a real Azure subscription on 2026-10-13. The discrepancies found then were fixed, and the items that could not be confirmed (Spot scale-up, running an upgrade, etc.) are listed in Appendix A. After the guide was translated into English, the same end-to-end run was repeated on 2026-10-14 with the same results. Results can differ with your subscription's quotas, organization policies, and regional capacity, so read the terraform plan output carefully the first time you run it. After the labs, be sure to clean up with Lab 11 (a cluster left running keeps costing money).

Architecture overview#

The stacks are split by lifecycle. Each later stack picks up the results of the earlier ones by looking them up through the naming convention (modules/naming).

Quick start#

Follow the detailed steps starting from Lab 01. The single-file HTML guide is published online; you can also open aks-terraform-guide.html from this repository in a browser (works offline; supports search, copy buttons, dark mode, and progress checkboxes).

Languages#

The guide is available in English (default) and Korean: the Korean edition lives in README.ko.md, labs/ko/, and aks-terraform-guide.ko.html. Terraform code, comments, and script messages are English-only, because both editions embed the same source files verbatim.

Lab scripts#

The check, verify, and delete commands you would otherwise type by hand are bundled into scripts (macOS · Linux · WSL · Cloud Shell; required: terraform az jq, plus kubectl kubelogin from Lab 05 on).

Script Purpose
scripts/preflight.sh Pre-start check: tools · sign-in · resource providers · vCPU quota · VM size · permissions (read-only)
scripts/verify.sh [stack…] Verifies the result after you apply each stack (read-only; ✓ ✗ ! summary and exit code)
scripts/cleanup.sh Deletes in the reverse order of creation · removes locks · checks for leftover resources (preview with --dry-run first)
tools/validate-all.sh fmt · validate · terraform test + script syntax checks, without Azure

Repository layout#

Validation and regenerating the HTML#

Pushing to main runs the same npm run build on a clean checkout in GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/pages.yml) and publishes the two HTML guides to GitHub Pages. The site is always built from the pushed sources, so run the build locally only if you want to refresh the offline copies of the HTML files in this repository.

Lab 00

AWS ↔ Azure infrastructure services compared (for EKS engineers)#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
30 min read None (none) None

This document puts the service, concept, and Terraform differences in one place so that engineers who are familiar with AWS (EKS, VPC, IAM …) can get up to speed on Azure and AKS quickly. The code in every later lab carries comments that map each piece back to AWS (for example # Equivalent to … or AWS comparison: …), so come back to these tables whenever you get stuck.

ℹ️Note

Official comparison resources: Azure for AWS professionals and AKS for Amazon EKS professionals (maintained by Microsoft). The tables in this guide are based on those resources and the latest AKS documentation (as of 2026-10), trimmed to the parts the labs need.

1. Ten mindset shifts to make first#

# AWS intuition Azure approach
1 An account is the isolation, billing, and permission boundary The subscription is the billing and quota boundary, and the resource group (RG) is the unit of lifecycle, permissions, and deletion. Every resource must live inside an RG.
2 You write IAM users, roles, and policy JSON yourself Microsoft Entra ID (the directory) + Azure RBAC: a role assignment ties together "who (principal) + which role + at what scope". You mostly use built-in roles.
3 A subnet belongs to a single AZ A subnet spans the whole region, and the availability zone (AZ) is a property of the resource, such as a VM, node pool, or load balancer.
4 Security Group (stateful) + NACL (stateless) A single NSG does both jobs: it is stateful, rules have priorities (the lower the number, the earlier it is evaluated), and it supports both Allow and Deny. Attach it to a subnet or a NIC.
5 Private subnet + NAT Gateway (edit the route table) Attach the NAT Gateway directly to the subnet. No route table is needed, and relying on the default outbound IP is being phased out.
6 Gateway/Interface VPC Endpoint Private Endpoint (assigns a private IP to the service) + a Private DNS Zone that you configure yourself. There is no automatic "Enable Private DNS" option.
7 Role + trust policy Create a Managed Identity (UAMI), an identity that exists as a resource, and add a role assignment on the target resource. No keys or secrets.
8 S3 + DynamoDB for Terraform state locking Blob Storage alone is enough: locking is handled automatically by a blob lease, and authentication uses Entra ID (RBAC).
9 Most services need no separate activation Each subscription needs Resource Provider (RP) registration (Microsoft.ContainerService, etc.). azurerm 5.x does not register providers automatically.
10 With EKS, the nodes (EC2) show up directly in your account AKS nodes are created in a separate node resource group (MC_... or a name you specify) that AKS manages.

2. Organization, accounts, and regions#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
AWS Organizations root Entra tenant + root management group The tenant is the directory (users and apps); management groups are the hierarchy that groups subscriptions.
OU Management group Policies and role assignments are inherited by the subscriptions below.
Account Subscription The unit of quota (vCPU, etc.) and billing. Check the vCPU quota per region and per VM family in advance.
(none) Resource group A container that groups resources with the same lifecycle. Deleting it deletes every resource inside. Also used as a scope for tags, locks, and RBAC.
SCP Azure Policy + RBAC An SCP is a permission ceiling, whereas Azure Policy is a set of rules that evaluate and enforce resource properties (audit, deny, automatic remediation).
Region / AZ Region / Availability Zone koreacentral provides 3 AZs. Zone numbers (1, 2, 3) can map to different physical AZs in each subscription.
Resource ARN Resource ID Takes the form /subscriptions/<id>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/<RP>/<type>/<name>. In Terraform, resources reference each other through id.
Tags Tags Tag keys are case-insensitive. Resource group tags are not inherited automatically (Policy can add inheritance). Use tags as filters in cost analysis.

3. Networking#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
VPC Virtual Network (VNet) Regional. Can have multiple address spaces.
Subnet (tied to one AZ) Subnet (not tied to an AZ) You can apply a delegation to a subnet so that a specific service (such as the AKS API server) uses it exclusively.
Security Group / NACL NSG, ASG (Application Security Group) An NSG attaches to a subnet or NIC. An ASG lets you use a "logical group" in rules, much like an SG reference.
Internet Gateway (no separate resource) Having a public IP gives internet connectivity. For outbound traffic, explicitly specify one of NAT, load balancer, or firewall.
NAT Gateway + EIP NAT Gateway + Public IP The StandardV2 SKU is zone-redundant. Attach it to a subnet.
VPC Endpoint (Interface) Private Endpoint Each PaaS service needs its own privatelink.* Private DNS Zone.
VPC Endpoint (Gateway: S3/DDB) Service Endpoint Routes traffic from the subnet to the PaaS public endpoint over the Azure backbone. Private Endpoint is recommended for new designs.
Route 53 (Public/Private zone) Azure DNS, Private DNS Zone A Private Zone defines its resolution scope through VNet links.
ALB / NLB Application Gateway (L7), Azure Load Balancer (L4), Front Door (global L7) On AKS, a Gateway API implementation or Application Gateway for Containers is the counterpart of the ALB Controller.
Transit Gateway / VPC Peering VNet Peering, Virtual WAN Hub-and-spoke: Azure Firewall/Bastion/VPN in the hub, workloads in the spokes.
Network Firewall Azure Firewall To keep costs down, this lab uses a NAT Gateway; the firewall setup is covered in the appendix.
VPC Flow Logs VNet Flow Logs Creation of new NSG flow logs has been discontinued, and they have been replaced by VNet flow logs.
❗Important

IP planning changes. The VPC CNI in EKS consumes a VPC IP for every pod, but Azure CNI Overlay, the recommended AKS configuration, uses VNet IPs only for nodes and gives pods a separate CIDR (pod_cidr). The pod CIDR only has to avoid overlapping with the VNet and on-premises ranges.

4. Identity, permissions, and secrets#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
IAM User/Group Entra ID users/groups Sign-in, MFA, and Conditional Access are managed in Entra.
IAM Role (assumed by people or services) Managed Identity (granted to a resource) + service principal System-assigned (same lifetime as the resource) / User-assigned (UAMI, a standalone resource). UAMI is recommended for AKS.
IAM Policy (JSON) Role Definition + Role Assignment Pick a built-in role (Contributor, AcrPull …) → assign it at a scope. Custom roles are JSON too.
Permission boundary (none) / Azure Policy, ABAC conditions Partially implemented with assignment conditions (ABAC).
STS AssumeRole Token issuance (Entra) Apps obtain tokens automatically through the SDK's DefaultAzureCredential.
Instance profile Managed Identity (VM/VMSS) The node (kubelet) identity corresponds to this.
IRSA / EKS Pod Identity Microsoft Entra Workload ID The cluster's OIDC issuer + a federated credential (issuer+subject) + the SA annotation azure.workload.identity/client-id. The structure is almost identical to IRSA.
KMS Key Vault (Keys) / Managed HSM Manages service encryption keys (CMK).
Secrets Manager / Parameter Store Key Vault (Secrets) / App Configuration On AKS, mount them with the Secrets Store CSI Driver.
ACM Key Vault (Certificates) / App Service certificates Gateway TLS certificates are synced from Key Vault.
CloudTrail Activity Log + Diagnostic settings The management plane is covered by the Activity Log; the data plane (such as Key Vault access) is sent to Log Analytics through diagnostic settings.

5. Containers and Kubernetes (EKS ↔ AKS)#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
EKS (Standard) AKS Standard The control plane is managed in both. The uptime SLA starts with the AKS Standard tier (paid).
EKS Auto Mode AKS Automatic A mode that hands nodes, scaling, upgrades, and even security defaults over to the platform. As of 2026, Microsoft recommends "Automatic for most new production workloads" → Lab 10.
Managed node group (ASG) Node pool (VMSS) Separate the System pool (system pods such as CoreDNS) from the User pool (apps). At least 3 nodes / 4 vCPUs are recommended for the System pool.
Karpenter Node Auto Provisioning (NAP) AKS runs Karpenter as a managed service. Optional on Standard, default on Automatic.
Cluster Autoscaler Cluster Autoscaler min/max per node pool. Balances pools across availability zones (balance_similar_node_groups).
Fargate Virtual nodes (ACI) / Container Apps AKS has no 1:1 equivalent for serverless pods, so consider a separate service.
ECR ACR Private Endpoint, geo-replication, and zone redundancy require Premium. Nodes get pull permission through the AcrPull role.
VPC CNI Azure CNI Overlay + Cilium Cilium (eBPF) replaces kube-proxy and the NetworkPolicy implementation. kubenet is not recommended for new clusters.
AWS Load Balancer Controller (ALB) App Routing Gateway API (approuting-istio), Application Gateway for Containers ingress-nginx maintenance ended in 2026-03 → move to Gateway API → Lab 07.
EBS CSI / EFS CSI Azure Disk CSI / Azure Files CSI Installed and enabled by default.
EKS access entries (replacing aws-auth) Azure RBAC for Kubernetes (+ Kubernetes RBAC) Turning off local accounts (static kubeconfig) is recommended. Sign in with tokens through kubelogin.
EKS control plane logging Diagnostic settings (kube-audit-admin, kube-apiserver …) Sent to Log Analytics. kube-audit is high-volume, so kube-audit-admin is recommended.
EKS upgrades (manual / Extended Support) Auto-upgrade channels (patch, stable …) + maintenance window 12 months of support. From 2027-06, the platform automatically upgrades versions that are out of support.
Container Insights / AMP / AMG Container Insights (logs) / Managed Prometheus / Managed Grafana Unified under Azure Monitor. You connect the collection configuration through DCRs/DCRAs → Lab 05.
GuardDuty EKS / Inspector Microsoft Defender for Containers A subscription-level plan + a cluster profile.
AWS Config / Kyverno Azure Policy for Kubernetes (Gatekeeper) Assign policy initiatives at the RG or subscription scope → Lab 08.
EKS pricing: hourly fee per cluster AKS: Free / Standard / Premium tiers Free has no SLA. Standard has an hourly fee per cluster (check the official price list). Premium includes LTS.
💡Tip

The AKS node resource group: in addition to the cluster RG (for example, rg-...-aks), a separate node RG (rg-...-aks-nodes) is created that holds the VMSS, load balancers, and disks. Don't modify it directly (Automatic locks it down completely).

6. Storage and state#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
S3 Blob Storage (Storage account → Container) Account names must be globally unique (lowercase letters and digits, 3–24 characters). Versioning and soft delete are account-level options.
DynamoDB (lock) (not needed) The azurerm backend locks state with a blob lease.
EBS Managed Disk Premium SSD v2 / Ultra, etc. Ephemeral OS disks use the node's local storage.
EFS Azure Files (NFS/SMB) Included in the default AKS CSI drivers.

7. Cost management#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
Budgets Cost Management budgets azurerm_consumption_budget_subscription + tag filter → Lab 08.
Savings Plans / RI Reservations / Savings plan Can also be applied to node VMs.
Spot Instances Spot VM (Spot node pool) On eviction: Delete or Deallocate. Pods need a toleration.
Cost Explorer (EKS) AKS cost analysis add-on View costs per namespace/workload (cost_analysis_enabled).

8. Differences from a Terraform perspective#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
provider "aws" provider "azurerm" (+ azapi, azuread) azurerm = core resources, azapi = direct ARM API calls (new features and unsupported properties), azuread = Entra objects. azapi plays a role similar to AWS's awscc.
Credentials: AWS_PROFILE, SSO az login + ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID In CI, sign in without passwords through OIDC (workload identity federation).
terraform-aws-modules Azure Verified Modules (AVM) Official, verified modules. For learning purposes, this lab defines resources directly (consider AVM for production too).
tags on resources tags on resources + a resource group is required Almost every resource needs the resource_group_name argument.
S3 backend azurerm backend (use_azuread_auth = true) Uses Entra authentication/RBAC instead of key authentication.
Data source (data "aws_vpc") data "azurerm_virtual_network" To connect stacks, this lab uses a naming convention + data sources instead of remote state.
Deletion protection / Soft delete Key Vault soft-delete / purge protection, resource locks After terraform destroy, names can stay reserved for a while → Lab 11.
⚠️Warning

Key changes in azurerm 5.x (GA in 2026-07): the default for automatic Resource Provider registration is none, the node_provisioning_profile block of azurerm_kubernetes_cluster is now required, rbac_authorization_enabled of azurerm_key_vault is now required, and many enable_* arguments were renamed to *_enabled. If you copy 4.x code, you get errors at the terraform validate step.

9. Command cheat sheet#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
aws sts get-caller-identity az account show Check the current subscription, tenant, and user
aws configure sso / aws sso login az login Select a subscription with az account set --subscription <id>
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name x az aks get-credentials -g <rg> -n x + kubelogin convert-kubeconfig -l azurecli kubelogin handles the Entra sign-in
aws eks list-clusters / describe-cluster az aks list -o table / az aks show -g <rg> -n <name> The SKU column tells the two clusters of this guide apart: Base (Standard) and Automatic
kubectl config get-contexts / use-context The same commands Each az aks get-credentials makes that cluster the current context. With two clusters, check it before apply or delete (Appendix D)
(no direct equivalent) az aks command invoke -g <rg> -n <name> --command "kubectl …" Runs kubectl through the Azure API when there is no network path to the API server, for example from Cloud Shell (Appendix D)
(no direct equivalent; scale node groups to 0) az aks stop / az aks start Stops the nodes and their billing but keeps the cluster (Lab 09 section 4)
kubectl get/describe/logs/exec/scale/rollout The same kubectl Pods and Deployments are plain Kubernetes: see Appendix E
aws ecr get-login-password | docker login az acr login -n <acr> Use az acr import to copy an external image into ACR on the server side
aws ec2 describe-vpcs az network vnet list -o table Use -o table and --query (JMESPath)
aws iam list-attached-role-policies az role assignment list --assignee <id> --all -o table Look up role assignments
aws logs start-query az monitor log-analytics query -w <id> --analytics-query "…" Uses KQL
aws service-quotas get-service-quota az vm list-usage -l koreacentral -o table Quota per vCPU family
eksctl upgrade az aks get-upgrades -g <rg> -n <name> → az aks upgrade In this lab: patches go through the auto-upgrade channel, and minor versions through az aks upgrade after a preflight check (Lab 09). Terraform ignores the version after creation with ignore_changes (Lab 09 also describes how to manage the version in code).

10. Best practices this lab follows (summary)#

  • State/structure: stacks split by lifecycle (network → platform → aks → workload), remote state with Entra authentication, pinned provider versions, automated validation with terraform fmt/validate/test.
  • Networking: Azure CNI Overlay + Cilium, fixed egress through a NAT Gateway (StandardV2), default outbound access disabled on subnets, Private Endpoints (ACR/Key Vault).
  • Identity/security: UAMI + role assignments, local accounts disabled, Entra + Azure RBAC, Workload Identity, Key Vault RBAC and purge protection, ACR anonymous access and admin account disabled, Azure Policy, Defender.
  • Availability/operations: Standard tier (SLA), spread across 3 availability zones, separate System/User pools, PDB, HPA, and topology spread, maintenance window + automatic patch upgrades.
  • Observability: Managed Prometheus + Container Insights (DCR) + Managed Grafana, control plane diagnostic logs.
  • Cost: daily log cap, budget alerts, Spot pool (optional), terraform destroy after the lab.

Lab 01

Lab 01. Prerequisites: tools, sign-in, permissions, environment variables#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
20–30 min None (none) 00. AWS ↔ Azure comparison

Goals of this lab#

  • Install Azure CLI, Terraform, kubectl, kubelogin, and jq, and verify their versions

  • Sign in to Azure, select a subscription, and check the permissions you need

  • Register Resource Providers (RPs) and check your vCPU quota (AWS has no equivalent step)

  • Set the environment variables that every later lab shares

  • Check all of the above automatically with a single run of scripts/preflight.sh

  • You have an Azure subscription and Owner permission (or Contributor + User Access Administrator)

  • terraform version reports 1.16 or later

  • The azure-cli version in az version is 2.86 or later

  • kubectl, kubelogin, and jq are installed

  • scripts/preflight.sh finishes with no failures (✗)

1. Install the tools#

Tool Minimum version Purpose
Terraform 1.16 IaC (this guide is verified with 1.16.5)
Azure CLI 2.86 Sign-in, quota/RP queries, az acr import, az aks get-credentials
kubectl Cluster version ±1 minor Kubernetes CLI
kubelogin Latest Authenticates kubectl and the Terraform kubernetes provider with Entra ID tokens
jq Latest Used by the verification script (scripts/verify.sh) to read JSON output from az/kubectl
ℹ️Note

The shell scripts in scripts/ run on macOS · Linux · WSL · Azure Cloud Shell (bash). On Windows PowerShell, use WSL or Git Bash. Cloud Shell has one limit: its public IP is not in TF_VAR_allowed_ip_ranges, so the kubectl steps from Lab 05 on (and the Lab 06–07 stacks that use the kubernetes provider) cannot reach the API servers from there. Use az aks command invoke instead (Appendix D).

💡Tip

On any OS, if you have installed only the Azure CLI, a single az aks install-cli installs both kubectl and kubelogin.

2. Sign in and select a subscription#

This is the equivalent of aws sso login / AWS_PROFILE in AWS. Terraform uses your Azure CLI sign-in directly.

Required permissions#

Task Required Azure RBAC role Why
Create resources Contributor RG, VNet, AKS, ACR, and so on
Create role assignments User Access Administrator or Owner This lab creates many azurerm_role_assignment resources (AcrPull, Network Contributor …)
Assign policies (Lab 08) Resource Policy Contributor or Owner azurerm_resource_group_policy_assignment
ℹ️Note

This lab doesn't use the azuread provider (to create Entra groups, for example), so you don't need Entra ID administrator permissions. For lab convenience, human-facing permissions such as cluster admin (Labs 05/10) and ACR Push and Grafana Admin (Lab 04) are granted to "the currently signed-in user" as Azure RBAC roles (the grant_current_user_admin / grant_current_user_roles variables, default true). In team and CI environments, set these variables to false and specify the object IDs of Entra groups in admin_principal_ids. Granting permissions directly to personal accounts means the code has to change every time the person in charge changes.

3. Register Resource Providers#

In Azure, you must register the Resource Provider (RP) for each service in your subscription before you can create that service's resources. Starting with azurerm 5.x, the provider doesn't register RPs automatically (the default is none), so you register them manually, just once.

4. Check your vCPU quota#

The default configuration uses at least six D4ds_v5 (4 vCPU) nodes (3 System + 3 User), and upgrades create extra temporary (surge) nodes. The recommended headroom is 40 vCPUs (24 vCPUs minimum plus the surge nodes).

Quota (name in az vm list-usage) Required
standardDDSv5Family (family quota for D4ds_v5) 6 nodes = 24 → 28 with upgrade surge → 44 at the autoscale maximum (System 5 + User 6 = 11 nodes)
cores (Total Regional vCPUs, the sum of all families) The value above + the AKS Automatic nodes from Lab 10 (about 8), if you use both: 36 or more
Spot vCPUs (optional: the Spot pool in Lab 05) 5 nodes × 4 = 20. Counted separately from the regular vCPU quota
⚠️Warning

If restrictions contains NotAvailableForSubscription, you can't use that VM size/zone in your subscription. If your quota is too low, request an increase from the Quotas menu in the portal or through a support request, or change the system_node_vm_size/user_node_vm_size variables (Lab 05).

If your default quota is small, as with a Visual Studio subscription (for example, 20 for the family and 32 in total), you can request an increase from the CLI. A small increase is sometimes applied as soon as you request it, but this depends on the subscription type, so confirm that it took effect with the az vm list-usage command above.

Instead of requesting an increase, you can reduce system_node_vm_size/user_node_vm_size to Standard_D2ds_v5 (2 vCPU) and still do the lab within the same family quota (20): 6 nodes = 12 vCPUs.

5. Set environment variables#

These are the values that every stack reads. Run the commands again each time you open a new terminal (saving them to an env.sh file makes this easier).

❗Important

Your public IP changes if you use a corporate VPN/proxy or switch networks. Access to Key Vault, ACR, and the API servers is then blocked, so update TF_VAR_allowed_ip_ranges and apply the three stacks that use it again: 04-platform (ACR, Key Vault), 05-aks and 10-aks-automatic (API servers). See Appendix D. Do not run the command above inside Cloud Shell: it would register Cloud Shell's IP instead of your laptop's.

6. Check everything at once: the preflight script#

Instead of checking steps 3–5 above by hand one at a time, run the read-only preflight script. It doesn't create or change anything.

Check If it fails
Tools and versions (terraform 1.16+, az 2.86+, kubectl, kubelogin, jq) Install instructions are printed along with the failure message
Azure sign-in and subscription az login
Format of ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID and TF_VAR_allowed_ip_ranges Run the export commands from step 5 again
Whether the 17 required Resource Providers are registered Prints the registration command (az provider register …) ready to run
vCPU quota (D4ds_v5 family · whole region, minimum 24 / recommended 40) Request an increase in the portal
Whether the VM size is available in zones 1, 2, and 3 and has no restrictions Adjust the zones / VM size variables
Role assignment permissions, such as Owner Request permissions (permissions granted through a group may not be listed, so this is reported as a warning)
ℹ️Note

The common functions shared by the scripts (scripts/lib/common.sh) are in Appendix I. All the verification scripts report their results in the same format: ✓ passed / ✗ failed / ! warnings / - skipped.

7. Repository structure#

Each terraform/NN-* directory is an independent Terraform root module (= independent state). The code shown in the doc for lab N is identical to the files in the corresponding directory.

8. (Optional) Validate the code without Azure#

You can run fmt → validate → terraform test (mock provider) for every stack without signing in or having a subscription. The full run also includes a syntax check of the shell scripts in scripts/ (bash -n, plus shellcheck if it is installed).

Lab 02

Lab 02. Terraform remote state: S3 + DynamoDB ↔ Blob Storage#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
20 min Almost none terraform/02-bootstrap, terraform/modules/naming 01. Prerequisites

What you build in this lab#

You build a remote state store (a Storage Account + container) that every stack shares, and a shared module (naming) that makes every stack follow the same naming convention.

The state store has the following structure.

Comparison for AWS engineers#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
S3 bucket Storage Account + Blob container The Storage Account name must be globally unique (3–24 lowercase letters and digits).
DynamoDB lock table (not needed) The azurerm backend handles locking with a blob lease.
S3 Versioning blob_properties.versioning_enabled Roll back an accidentally overwritten state to a previous version.
Block Public Access allow_nested_items_to_be_public = false Blocks public access to containers.
IAM policy (s3:GetObject/PutObject) RBAC Storage Blob Data Contributor Data plane roles are separate. Contributor (a management plane role) alone can't read or write blobs.
Access keys/credentials shared_access_key_enabled = false + use_azuread_auth = true Turns off account keys entirely and allows only Entra ID authentication.
💡Tip

Why we split state per stack: The network (almost never changes) → platform services → cluster → workloads differ in how often they change and in who is authorized to change them. Splitting state reduces the blast radius of a change and makes it less likely that you touch the VNet by accident. Stacks are linked through a naming convention + data sources instead of terraform_remote_state (you don't need to share access to the state files, and no circular dependencies arise).

Shared module: modules/naming#

In Azure, resource naming conventions (Cloud Adoption Framework abbreviations) and globally unique names (ACR, Key Vault, Storage) are a significant concern. This module builds a 5-character hash from subscription ID + workload + environment, so it reproduces the same names no matter which stack calls it.

terraform test is Terraform's built-in testing framework. Since this is pure logic with no provider, it runs right away.

Bootstrap stack code#

versions.tf — Pins the Terraform and provider versions (~> 5.9 = 5.9 or later, below 6). The commented-out backend block at the end is used in step 4 below.

providers.tf — azurerm 5.x doesn't register Resource Providers automatically (none).

main.tf — The storage account uses ZRS (zone-redundant), disables key authentication, and enables versioning and soft delete.

Step 5. Verify#

This runs the manual checks from step 5 (key authentication blocked, versioning, container, state files) in one go. It is read-only and returns a ✓ passed / ✗ failed / ! warnings summary and an exit code (1 if anything failed).

Common issues#

Symptom Cause / fix
AuthorizationPermissionMismatch (403 during init) Role assignment propagation delay. Retry after 1–5 minutes. Check that Storage Blob Data Contributor is assigned at the container/account scope.
StorageAccountAlreadyTaken The name is already taken globally. Changing TF_VAR_workload changes the hash.

Lab 03

Lab 03. Networking: VNet · NSG · NAT Gateway · Private DNS#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
20 min NAT Gateway + Public IP (small hourly charge) terraform/03-network 02. Remote state

What you build in this lab#

Here is the same design summarized as text:

Comparison for AWS engineers#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
VPC azurerm_virtual_network Subnet CIDRs can be chosen freely within the VNet address space. Azure reserves 5 IPs per subnet (same as AWS).
Subnet (tied to one AZ) azurerm_subnet Not tied to an AZ. Node pools and load balancers specify the AZ.
Security Group + NACL azurerm_network_security_group Stateful, with priorities (lower number wins) and Deny rules. Attached to a subnet.
Private subnet + NAT GW azurerm_nat_gateway + subnet association No route table changes needed. default_outbound_access_enabled = false turns off "implicit internet access".
Interface VPC Endpoint azurerm_private_endpoint + Private DNS Zone Connected to ACR/Key Vault in the next lab, Lab 04.
Route 53 Private Hosted Zone azurerm_private_dns_zone + ..._virtual_network_link Names resolve in a VNet only if the zone has a link to that VNet.
❗Important

IP capacity planning: With Azure CNI Overlay, only nodes use VNet IPs. A /24 node subnet (251 IPs) is plenty for a few dozen nodes, even counting the temporary nodes created during upgrades (max_surge 33%). If you plan for hundreds of nodes, grow it to /22 or larger. The API server subnet needs at least a /28 per cluster, and it can't be used for anything else.

Design decisions (best practices)#

Decision Why
Separate subnets by purpose (nodes / API server / ingress / Private Endpoints) You can plan NSGs, delegation, and IPs per subnet. Keeping the ingress LB IPs in their own subnet means they don't affect the node subnet rules.
default_outbound_access_enabled = false The default outbound IP isn't owned by you and can change, and Azure is in the process of retiring it. Explicit egress (NAT Gateway) is the recommended approach.
NAT Gateway StandardV2 Zone-redundant, and usable with AKS userAssignedNATGateway. Not supported in some regions (e.g., Canada East) → set the variable nat_gateway_sku = "Standard".
Private Endpoint subnet NSG: allow only port 443 from the node subnet + deny all other VNet-internal traffic Applying an NSG to Private Endpoints requires private_endpoint_network_policies = "Enabled". Least-privilege network separation.
Node subnet NSG: define the inbound allow rules directly in Terraform AKS doesn't modify an NSG that you create yourself and attach to a subnet (it doesn't add rules for Services automatically either). Without this rule, a public Gateway can't be reached. Pod and API server traffic passes under the default rules, but it breaks the moment you add a Deny rule, so the allow rules are created up front (all verified in a real subscription). See NSG inbound rules below.
Ingress subnet NSG has no rules This subnet holds only the internal LB frontend IP and has no VMs (NICs). Traffic that passes through the load balancer is evaluated by the node subnet NSG, which is the backend.
Manage the Private DNS Zones in the network stack In real environments they are often managed centrally in the Connectivity subscription.

NSG inbound rules#

An NSG evaluates rules from the lowest priority number upward, and if no rule matches, it applies the default rules (AllowVnetInBound 65000 → AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound 65001 → DenyAllInBound 65500). The inbound traffic in this stack and how each flow is allowed are listed below. The results in the Category column were confirmed in a real subscription by deleting rules or adding a Deny rule (Appendix A).

NSG Traffic Rule Category
Node Node ↔ node · clients inside the VNet → internal Gateway Default rule AllowVnetInBound Passes via default rule
Node Azure Load Balancer health probes Default rule AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound Passes via default rule
Node Internet → public Gateway (HTTP/HTTPS) AllowGatewayHttpHttps (200): gateway_allowed_source_prefixes (default Internet) → TCP 80 · 443 Required — deleting it blocks access
Node Node → pod · pod ↔ pod (including DNS) AllowNodesToPods (100): node CIDR → pod_cidr · AllowPodsToPods (110): pod_cidr → pod_cidr Defensive — passes via default rules; breaks if you add a Deny
Node API server → node (kubelet 10250: kubectl exec · logs) · pod AllowApiServerToCluster (120): API server subnet → node CIDR · pod_cidr Defensive — passes via default rules; exec breaks if you add a Deny
Private Endpoint Node → ACR · Key Vault AllowAksNodesHttps (100): node CIDR → TCP 443. All other VNet traffic is denied by DenyOtherVnetInbound (4000) Design
Ingress None No rules are defined (see Design decisions above) —
❗Important

AKS doesn't modify an NSG that you create yourself and attach to a subnet. Rules for Services (LoadBalancer) are added automatically only to resources that AKS manages (AKS networking concepts). In practice, AKS creates its own NSG (aks-agentpool-…-nsg) in the node resource group, attaches it to the node NICs, and adds the k8s-azure-lb_allow_… rules only there, while our subnet NSG is left untouched. Inbound traffic has to pass both the subnet NSG and the NIC NSG, so without an allow rule in the subnet NSG, the public Gateway isn't reachable.

❗Important

Pod traffic is also evaluated by the subnet NSG. Pod traffic in Azure CNI Overlay isn't encapsulated, so the subnet NSG applies to it (Azure CNI Overlay: NSG). With only the default rules, cross-node pod communication and DNS pass through unchanged, but both break the moment a Deny rule is added (e.g., a priority 4000 Deny), such as through organizational policy or hardening. With AllowNodesToPods / AllowPodsToPods in place, traffic passes even when a Deny rule exists. That's why pod_cidr must be the same value as in 05-aks (default 10.244.0.0/16), and scripts/verify.sh 05-aks checks that the two values match.

ℹ️Note

To open the public Gateway to specific IPs only, pass -var 'gateway_allowed_source_prefixes=["203.0.113.10/32"]'; if you use only an internal Gateway, pass -var 'gateway_allowed_source_prefixes=[]' (no rule is created). Port 443 is allowed up front so that you don't have to edit the NSG again when you add the TLS listener in Lab 07.

No NSG is attached to snet-aks-apiserver (it's a delegated subnet, and traffic inside the VNet is allowed by default). If you attach one, first allow these inbound rules: node subnet → API server subnet on TCP 443 · 4443, and AzureLoadBalancer → API server subnet on TCP 9988 (API Server VNet Integration).

Unit tests (verify the plan logic with terraform test, no Azure needed)

Common issues#

Symptom Cause / fix
SubnetsHaveNoAddressPrefixes / CIDR conflict Set an address_space that doesn't overlap with your on-premises or peered VNets.
StandardV2 NAT gateway is not supported in region Use -var nat_gateway_sku=Standard (in this case zones = ["1"], a single zone).
Connections to the Private Endpoint subnet fail Check the NSG rule priorities (100 allow → 4000 deny) and the source (node subnet CIDR).
Cross-node pod communication and DNS don't work (after Lab 05) Check that no Deny rule was added to the node NSG, and that AllowPodsToPods covers the same range as pod_cidr in 05-aks. If they differ, make pod_cidr the same in both stacks and apply 03-network again.
kubectl exec · logs fail with connection reset / timeout If the node NSG has a Deny rule, check that AllowApiServerToCluster (API server subnet → node port 10250) is still there.
The public Gateway times out (Lab 07) Check that the node NSG has AllowGatewayHttpHttps and that gateway_allowed_source_prefixes includes your IP (az network nsg rule list). An internal Gateway can't be reached from outside the VNet.

Lab 04. Platform services: ACR · Key Vault · monitoring · identities for AKS#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
30 min ACR Premium + Managed Grafana + Private Endpoint (about $0.2–0.3 per hour) terraform/04-platform 03. Networking

What you build in this lab#

Before the cluster itself, you create the shared services it "depends on" and the two managed identities that AKS will use.

Comparison for AWS engineers#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
ECR azurerm_container_registry (ACR) Private Endpoint, IP firewall, and zone redundancy are Premium features. Nodes pull images with the AcrPull role. admin_enabled = false.
ECR lifecycle policy retention_policy_in_days (untagged manifests) Premium feature.
EKS cluster role / node role Two UAMIs + role assignments AWS attaches a trust policy and a permissions policy to a role, whereas Azure works as "identity resource → role assignment on the target resource".
KMS + Secrets Manager + ACM azurerm_key_vault rbac_authorization_enabled = true → the same RBAC model as IAM. A required argument in 5.x.
VPC Endpoint (Interface) azurerm_private_endpoint + private_dns_zone_group An A record is registered automatically in the Private DNS Zone from Lab 03.
CloudWatch Logs Log Analytics workspace Query with KQL. A daily ingestion cap (daily_quota_gb) prevents runaway costs.
Amazon Managed Prometheus (AMP) azurerm_monitor_workspace Compatible with Prometheus remote write/query. Collection is configured through the DCR/DCRA in Lab 05.
Amazon Managed Grafana (AMG) azurerm_dashboard_grafana Grafana sign-in uses Entra ID. You must be assigned the Grafana Admin role to see dashboards.
💡Tip

Why create the UAMIs yourself? AKS also supports a system-assigned identity, but if you create the UAMIs in advance and finish the role assignments first, cluster creation is less likely to fail because of permission propagation delays, and the identities and permissions survive even if you recreate the cluster. Separating the kubelet identity also lets you finish the ACR permissions before the cluster is created.

Role assignments at a glance#

Principal Role Scope Why
cluster UAMI Network Contributor Network RG Join subnets, use the NAT Gateway, allocate internal LB IPs
cluster UAMI Managed Identity Operator kubelet UAMI Attach the kubelet identity to the nodes
kubelet UAMI AcrPull ACR Pull images
Lab user (current user) AcrPush ACR Push / import images (grant_current_user_roles; for teams/CI, set it to false and grant the role separately to a group or CI principal)
Grafana MI Monitoring Data Reader Azure Monitor workspace Query Prometheus
Lab user Grafana Admin Grafana Sign in to dashboards (grant_current_user_roles)

Design decisions (best practices)#

Decision Why
Put ACR/Key Vault behind a Private Endpoint, and allow only your IP (plus trusted Azure services) on the public endpoint (default Deny) Nodes and pods reach them only over the private path. Admin PCs and CI can run az acr import and create secrets through the IP allow rule. The firewall's "Allow trusted Azure services" option (Key Vault bypass = "AzureServices", ACR network_rule_bypass_option defaulting to AzureServices) is turned on, so to lock it down completely, change it to "None". In production, put CI runners inside the VNet and turn public access off entirely.
Key Vault purge protection + 7-day soft delete Prevents accidental deletion. But after destroy, the name stays reserved for 7 days (if you recreate it with the same name, the provider recovers it) → Lab 11.
Strip /32 from Key Vault IP rules Key Vault doesn't accept /31 or /32; you must write a single IP instead (replace(cidr, "/32", "")).
ACR admin_enabled = false, anonymous_pull_enabled = false Removes static credentials and anonymous access.
Log Analytics local_authentication_enabled = false Allows only Entra (managed identity) authentication instead of shared keys.
Collect ACR/Key Vault audit logs with diagnostic settings Plays the same role as CloudTrail data events.

Code#

identity.tf — the UAMIs that AKS uses, and their role assignments

registry.tf — ACR + Private Endpoint + diagnostic settings

keyvault.tf

observability.tf — Log Analytics, Azure Monitor workspace, Managed Grafana

ℹ️Note

If you'd rather not deploy Grafana, run export TF_VAR_enable_grafana=false first. It doesn't affect how the cluster works, and Prometheus collection in Lab 05 still works.

Automated verification script#

Common issues#

Symptom Cause / fix
MissingSubscriptionRegistration The resource provider isn't registered → step 3 of Lab 01. Check Microsoft.Dashboard and Microsoft.Monitor in particular.
az acr import fails with 403/denied Public access is allowed only from the IPs in allowed_ip_ranges. Check whether your current IP has changed, then run terraform apply.
az keyvault secret set fails with Forbidden The Key Vault firewall (IP) or a data plane role (Key Vault Secrets Officer) is missing. Role propagation can take a few minutes.
Grafana ZoneRedundancy/version error As of azurerm 5.9, grafana_major_version can be 12 or 13. If the region has constraints, use enable_grafana=false.
Key Vault name already exists (soft-deleted) The provider's recover_soft_deleted_key_vaults = true recovers it. If it was deleted earlier with purge protection on, the only option for 7 days is to recover it.

Lab 05

Lab 05. AKS cluster (Standard): how it differs from EKS#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
40 min (apply 15–25 min) About $1.7–2 per hour (Standard tier + 6 or more nodes) terraform/05-aks 04. Platform services

What you build in this lab#

Comparison for EKS engineers#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
aws_eks_cluster azurerm_kubernetes_cluster Both control planes are managed. The uptime SLA starts at sku_tier = "Standard" (the Free tier has no SLA).
aws_eks_node_group / ASG default_node_pool + azurerm_kubernetes_cluster_node_pool You separate the System pool (required, for system pods only) from the User pool. Nodes = VMSS.
Nodes are EC2 instances in your VPC Node resource group (node_resource_group) The VMSS, load balancer, and disks are created in an RG separate from the cluster RG. Don't modify them directly.
VPC CNI (pod = VPC IP) network_plugin = azure + network_plugin_mode = overlay Pods use pod_cidr → saves VNet IPs. You can't reach pod IPs directly from outside the cluster (use Pod Subnet mode if you need that).
(Install Calico/Cilium separately) network_data_plane = cilium, network_policy = cilium Managed Cilium. Replaces kube-proxy + enforces NetworkPolicy + (optional) ACNS observability/security.
Public/private endpoint + CIDR restriction api_server_access_profile (VNet Integration + authorized_ip_ranges) / private_cluster_enabled VNet Integration projects the API server into an internal load balancer (ILB) in your subnet (no private endpoint or DNS zone needed).
aws-auth ConfigMap / access entries azure_active_directory_role_based_access_control + role assignments Azure RBAC for Kubernetes: roles such as "Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin" control Kubernetes permissions too.
(No local admin) local_account_disabled = true By default, AKS has a static-certificate kubeconfig (the local account) → always turn it off.
IRSA / Pod Identity oidc_issuer_enabled + workload_identity_enabled Lab 06. In azurerm 5.x, the OIDC issuer defaults to true.
EKS upgrades kubernetes_version (at creation) + automatic_upgrade_channel + maintenance_window_* AKS applies patches automatically during the maintenance window; for minor versions, run a preflight check first, then upgrade step by step with az aks upgrade (Lab 09). After creation AKS manages the version, so Terraform ignores version changes (ignore_changes).
Karpenter / Cluster Autoscaler auto_scaler_profile (CA) / node_provisioning_profile (NAP) This lab uses the Cluster Autoscaler (mode = "Manual"). You try NAP in Lab 10 (Automatic).

Design decisions (best practices)#

Setting Value Why (WAF / baseline architecture recommendations)
sku_tier Standard Uptime SLA and the cost analysis add-on. Required for production.
kubernetes_version "1.36" (latest GA as of 2026-10) This is a minor alias at creation time. AKS manages later patch/minor versions, so lifecycle { ignore_changes } stops Terraform from reverting them (this prevents a permanent diff caused by the alias differing from the actual patch version). The AKS default is 1.35, and N-1 (1.35) is also a good choice for conservative operations. 1.37 is due to go GA (currently in preview). A check block warns if the region doesn't support the version.
automatic_upgrade_channel / node_os_upgrade_channel patch / NodeImage Security patches are applied automatically during the maintenance window; you run minor upgrades yourself after a preflight check (Lab 09). Control the timing with maintenance_window_*.
System pool D4ds_v5 ×3 (1 per zone), only_critical_addons_enabled Separates system pods from apps and tolerates a zone failure. 4 vCPUs or more recommended.
User pool D4ds_v5 ×3–6 (autoscaler) Apps only. A minimum of 3 nodes (the pool spans 3 zones, so one node per zone is typical) keeps the apps available even if a zone fails. Zone balance when the autoscaler scales out is best-effort. If you need strict balance, create a separate pool per zone and use balance_similar_node_groups.
OS AzureLinux3 + Ephemeral OS disk (64GB) Lightweight, hardened OS; fast node replacement; no disk cost. (Azure Linux 2.0 images are removed on 2026-10-31)
Networking CNI Overlay + Cilium, userAssignedNATGateway Saves IPs, eBPF data plane, fixed egress IP. kubenet isn't recommended for new clusters.
API server VNet Integration + authorized IP ranges Public, but reachable only from your IP. You can switch to a fully private cluster with enable_private_cluster = true (see the advanced experiments below).
Authentication Entra + Azure RBAC, local_account_disabled = true Access only through auditable identities. No static kubeconfig.
Add-ons Azure Policy, Key Vault CSI, Image Cleaner, KEDA, VPA, Cost analysis Governance, secrets, and cost visibility.
Observability Managed Prometheus + Container Insights (DCR) + control plane diagnostic logs Collects mainly kube-audit-admin (cheap). Prometheus recording rules support the default Grafana dashboards.
Not included Azure Firewall egress, App Gateway+WAF, multi-region Cost/complexity. See the "production checklist" in the appendix.
❗Important

Changes between azurerm 4.x and 5.x: The node_provisioning_profile { mode = "Manual" } block is required in 5.x (without it, validate fails). The oidc_issuer_enabled default is true in 5.x, enable_auto_scaling in default_node_pool was renamed to auto_scaling_enabled, and changing os_disk_type/only_critical_addons_enabled/vm_size and similar attributes requires temporary_name_for_rotation.

ℹ️Note

Why we use AzAPI: azurerm 5.9 doesn't yet expose the settings for control plane metrics and Gateway API (Managed Gateway API CRDs + the application routing Istio implementation). AzAPI's azapi_update_resource applies a partial update to the same cluster. The two updates are serialized with depends_on so they never PUT to the same cluster at the same time.

Code#

main.tf — lookups of resources from earlier stacks, the version check, and the resource group

cluster.tf — the cluster and node pools (the core of this lab)

monitoring.tf — Managed Prometheus / Container Insights / diagnostic settings

prometheus-rules.tf — the recording rules used by the default Grafana dashboards (copy and use as is)

gateway-api.tf — enable Gateway API with AzAPI

access.tf — human access to the cluster (lab: the current user / team: an Entra group)

💡Tip

By default, the "currently signed-in principal" that runs Terraform becomes the administrator (grant_current_user_admin = true). For teams and CI, run with grant_current_user_admin = false + admin_principal_ids = ["<Entra group Object ID>"] so that access doesn't shift when the principal running Terraform (a person or a pipeline) changes. If you leave both empty, the cluster would have no administrator, so a validation block prevents it.

Walkthrough#

Step 1. Plan and apply#

What to check in the plan output:

  • No check.kubernetes_version_is_supported warning appears (a warning lists the supported versions)
  • The network_profile, api_server_access_profile, and identity values of azurerm_kubernetes_cluster.this connect to the results of Labs 03/04
  • Resource count: 15 — resource group, cluster, User node pool, DCE 1 · DCR 2 · DCRA 2 (Prometheus / Container Insights), 2 Prometheus rule groups, diagnostic setting, 2 AzAPI updates, 2 role assignments
ℹ️Note

During apply, azapi_update_resource updates the cluster one more time, so the total time gets longer. Use the wait to re-read Design decisions.

Step 2. Get the kubeconfig (Entra ID sign-in)#

ℹ️Note

Use eval "$(…)", not a bare $(…). The output is a command line that contains &&, and a bare $(…) hands the && to az as an argument, so it fails with unrecognized arguments.

💡Tip

Local accounts are disabled, so the --admin option doesn't work. kubectl gets a token from your az login session, and your permissions come from the Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin role granted in access.tf of Lab 05. Role propagation can take 1–5 minutes (if you get Forbidden, retry after a moment). Every az aks get-credentials makes that cluster the current kubectl context. Once you also have the Lab 10 cluster, check kubectl config current-context (Appendix D).

Step 3. Verify#

Expected result: 6 or more nodes (system 3 + user 3), kubectl auth can-i → yes, GatewayClass approuting-istio shows ACCEPTED True, and the two outbound IPs are the same (egress goes through your NAT Gateway).

Step 4. Check observability#

It takes 5–10 minutes for data to accumulate.

In Grafana (the grafana_endpoint from Lab 04), open Dashboards → Azure Managed Prometheus → Kubernetes / Compute Resources / Cluster. If node and pod CPU/memory show up, it's working.

Advanced experiments#

(a) Add a Spot node pool#

(b) Switch to a fully private cluster#

Run terraform plan -var enable_private_cluster=true. Changing private_cluster_enabled recreates the cluster (forces replacement). In production, decide this from the start. With a private cluster, kubectl and the Terraform kubernetes provider can connect only from inside the VNet (VPN, Bastion, or a jump host). For an ad-hoc check, use az aks command invoke.

command invoke also works on the public cluster of this lab when you are on an address that is not in allowed_ip_ranges, such as Cloud Shell or another network (Appendix D).

Automated verification script#

A single az aks show call checks the cluster settings (security · networking · upgrades · add-ons · node pools), and kubectl checks the nodes, permissions, GatewayClass, and add-on pods. It uses a temporary kubeconfig, so ~/.kube/config isn't changed.

💡Tip

If the kubectl step fails with "Couldn't reach the API server", it's almost always because your public IP changed (or you are on another network or in Cloud Shell). Update TF_VAR_allowed_ip_ranges and apply 05-aks again; the IP list is also used by 04-platform and 10-aks-automatic (Appendix D). Settings you changed from the default setup (sku_tier, enable_gateway_api, node counts, the Lab 09 upgrade channel) are shown as values, warnings, or skips instead of ✗. For a private cluster (enable_private_cluster), the script skips the kubectl step when you run it from outside the VNet.

Common issues#

Symptom Cause / Fix
QuotaExceeded / Operation could not be completed as it results in exceeding approved ... cores Not enough vCPU quota → step 4 of Lab 01. Reduce the size/count or request a quota increase.
SkuNotAvailable, ZonalAllocationFailed The VM size is out of stock or restricted in that zone. Reduce var.zones to ["1","2"] or change *_node_vm_size.
AuthorizationFailed ... subnets/join/action Propagation delay, or a missing Network Contributor role from Lab 04. Retry after 5 minutes.
Unable to connect to the server: ... i/o timeout Your public IP changed, or you are on another network or in Cloud Shell → update TF_VAR_allowed_ip_ranges, then run terraform apply (and see Appendix D; az aks command invoke works meanwhile).
error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized) Run az login again, then kubelogin convert-kubeconfig -l azurecli.
Forbidden: ... cannot list resource Wait for Azure RBAC role propagation (up to 5 minutes). Or, if you applied with grant_current_user_admin = false, check that your own (or your group's) Object ID is in admin_principal_ids.
A default_node_pool.* change in terraform plan requires replacing the node pool Because temporary_name_for_rotation is set, the pool is replaced by rotation. System pods are briefly rescheduled during the replacement.
Prometheus is empty Check the ama-metrics pod status and the DCRA association (az monitor data-collection rule association list --resource <cluster-id>).

Next → Lab 06. Workload Identity + Key Vault CSI

← PreviousLab 04. Platform services: ACR · Key Vault · monitoring · identities for AKSNext →Lab 06. Workload Identity + Key Vault CSI: the Azure version of IRSA
Lab 06

Lab 06. Workload Identity + Key Vault CSI: the Azure version of IRSA#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
25 min Almost none (1 pod) terraform/06-workload 05. AKS cluster

What you build in this lab#

This is the complete flow for a pod to read a Key Vault secret without any static credentials (keys or passwords).

Here is the Azure side of the flow, step by step:

Comparison for AWS engineers#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
IAM OIDC Provider (registered per cluster) Cluster OIDC issuer (oidc_issuer_enabled) No separate registration is needed. You get the issuer URL from the oidc_issuer_url output.
IAM Role + trust policy (sub condition) UAMI + federated identity credential (issuer, subject, audience) An azurerm_federated_identity_credential resource replaces the trust policy JSON.
ServiceAccount annotation eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn Annotation azure.workload.identity/client-id The pod also needs the label azure.workload.identity/use: "true".
IAM Policy (secretsmanager:GetSecretValue) Role assignment Key Vault Secrets User (data plane) Management plane roles such as Contributor cannot read secret values.
Secrets Manager + CSI provider Key Vault provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver (AKS add-on) You declare the objects to fetch with the SecretProviderClass CRD. Supports an automatic refresh interval (secret_rotation_interval).
EKS Pod Identity (association API) (no equivalent) → Identity bindings for AKS A UAMI is limited to 20 federated credentials, so consider Identity bindings when several clusters share one identity.
❗Important

You can attach at most 20 federated credentials to a single UAMI. If you design for "one UAMI per app (namespace/SA)" by default, you rarely hit the limit and permissions stay minimal.

Design decisions (best practices)#

Decision Why
Kubernetes resources in a separate stack (06), applied once the cluster already exists Using the kubernetes provider in the same stack that creates the cluster means the provider configuration is only resolved at apply time, which makes planning and deletion error-prone.
kubernetes provider authentication = kubelogin + Azure CLI token Local accounts are disabled, so there are no static certificates or tokens. It is the same pattern as the aws eks get-token exec plugin for EKS.
A dedicated UAMI for the app, granted only Secrets User (read) Least privilege. Only humans (Secrets Officer) can write.
The secret value is ephemeral + write-only (value_wo) The value is never stored in the Terraform state (write-only arguments need Terraform 1.11+ and are supported in azurerm 5.x). To change the value, bump value_wo_version.
Pod Security restricted enforced on the namespace Enforces baseline security (non-root, no privilege escalation, seccomp, etc.) at the namespace level.
time_sleep to wait for RBAC propagation Prevents the common failure where a data plane call returns 403 right after a role assignment. depends_on makes both secret creation (operator permissions) and the pod's secret mount (app permissions + federated credential) run only after this wait.

Code#

providers.tf — the key part is how the kubernetes provider connects through kubelogin.

identity.tf — Azure side: UAMI, federated credential, role assignments, secret

kubernetes.tf — Kubernetes side: Namespace, ServiceAccount, SecretProviderClass, Deployment

Walkthrough#

Step 1. Import the demo image into ACR#

As with ECR's pull through cache, the best practice is to go through a private registry rather than pull external images directly. (Skip this step if you already did it in Lab 04.)

Step 2. Apply#

ℹ️Note

kubelogin and kubectl use your az login session. If you get an executable kubelogin not found error, check the tool installation in Lab 01.

Step 3. Verify#

If the two values match, it worked. Now take a look at what was injected.

iss is the oidc_issuer_url, sub is system:serviceaccount:demo:workload-sa, and aud is api://AzureADTokenExchange. The token exchange succeeds only if all three values match the federated credential.

Step 4. Check automatic secret refresh#

💡Tip

The app only picks up the new value when it re-reads the file. To use the secret as an environment variable, a common pattern is to sync a Kubernetes Secret through the CSI driver's secretObjects and pair it with a tool such as Reloader.

Step 5. (Optional) Check private DNS#

Check that nodes and pods resolve Key Vault and ACR to private IPs.

Automated verification script#

It checks the whole chain end to end: the Azure side (UAMI · federated credential issuer/subject · Key Vault role) and the Kubernetes side (ServiceAccount annotation · pod label · injected environment variables · mounted secret). It does not print the secret value.

Common issues#

Symptom Cause / Fix
AADSTS70021: No matching federated identity record found The federated credential's issuer/subject does not match. Check the namespace, the SA name, and oidc_issuer_url (including case and any trailing /).
AADSTS700211/AADSTS700213 The audience is not api://AzureADTokenExchange.
Pod stuck in ContainerCreating (failed to mount secrets store objects) The KV permission (Secrets User) has not propagated yet, the KV firewall is blocking access, or there is a typo in the SecretProviderClass clientID/tenantId/objects. Check the events in kubectl describe pod.
ImagePullBackOff az acr import was skipped, or the kubelet's AcrPull permission has not propagated yet.
kubernetes_manifest ... no matches for kind "SecretProviderClass" during plan The Key Vault CSI add-on is not enabled → check key_vault_secrets_provider in Lab 05.
Forbidden (creating the secret) Your current IP is not on the Key Vault firewall allow list → see allowed_ip_ranges in Lab 01/04.

Next → Lab 07. Ingress: Gateway API

← PreviousLab 05. AKS cluster (Standard): how it differs from EKSNext →Lab 07. Ingress: ALB Controller → Gateway API (approuting-istio)
Lab 07

Lab 07. Ingress: ALB Controller → Gateway API (approuting-istio)#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
30 min Public IP + load balancer + 3 pods (a small charge) terraform/07-ingress 05. AKS cluster

What you build in this lab#

Comparison for AWS engineers#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
ALB + AWS Load Balancer Controller (Ingress) Gateway API Gateway + HTTPRoute (GatewayClass approuting-istio) You declare routing, TLS and weights with standard API fields instead of Ingress annotations.
ALB listeners / rules / target groups Gateway.listeners / HTTPRoute.rules / backendRefs Separation of roles: Gateway (infrastructure) ↔ HTTPRoute (app).
internal vs. internet-facing scheme The Gateway's infrastructure.annotations (azure-load-balancer-internal) An internal LB uses a private IP from the snet-ingress subnet.
NLB (Service type=LoadBalancer) Azure Load Balancer Standard (Service type=LoadBalancer) L4. AKS manages it, with no separate controller to install.
AWS WAF Application Gateway (WAF v2) / Front Door WAF Putting it in front is the default architecture in the Microsoft baseline.
ACM certificates Key Vault certificates → synced with the Secrets Store CSI driver Used when you configure an HTTPS listener (see TLS below).
⚠️Warning

ingress-nginx has been retired. Maintenance of the community ingress-nginx ended in 2026-03, and Microsoft security patch support for the AKS application routing add-on (NGINX) also ends in 2026-11. Use Gateway API for new deployments. New AKS Automatic clusters (1.36+) use Gateway API by default.

Ingress options at a glance#

Option Characteristics When to use
App Routing Gateway API (this lab) Managed Istio control plane without sidecars, plus Envoy. It is upgraded together with AKS. Most HTTP/HTTPS ingress (header/body size limits, Lua, and rate limiting are not supported)
Application Gateway for Containers Fully managed L7 outside the cluster (closest to ALB), WAF integration You need high performance or WAF, or prefer L7 outside the cluster
Istio service mesh add-on + Gateway API Mesh features + ingress You need mTLS/traffic policies (cannot be used together with App Routing Gateway API)
Self-managed (Envoy Gateway, NGINX Gateway Fabric, etc.) Full control You need features the managed options do not support

Design decisions (best practices)#

Decision Why
Pull the app container from ACR (az acr import) Removes the dependency on public registry outages and rate limits, and allows image scanning and auditing. It also verifies the kubelet's AcrPull role and the Private Endpoint path directly.
Deployment: requests/limits, probes, non-root, capabilities drop, seccomp, zone spread (best-effort) A configuration that passes the Azure Policy baseline (Lab 08) and AKS Automatic's Deployment Safeguards. Because zone spread uses ScheduleAnyway, pods can pile into one zone when resources are short; DoNotSchedule can leave pods stuck in Pending during upgrades or failures, so it was deliberately not chosen.
PodDisruptionBudget + HPA(3~10) Keeps the app available during node upgrades and drains, and scales automatically with load.
NetworkPolicy: app pods allow only port 8080 from pods in the same namespace (web) Namespace-level isolation enforced by Cilium. Traffic from the Envoy proxy gets through because the proxy is created in the same namespace. ⚠️ pod_selector {} allows all pods in web. To narrow it down, check the actual labels of the Envoy pods with kubectl -n web get pods --show-labels and restrict to those labels. (Apply the NetworkPolicy only to the app pods; otherwise, Envoy's inbound traffic from outside gets blocked.)
Namespace PSS: enforce baseline + warn on restricted The Envoy proxy pods are created in the same namespace, so enforce stays at baseline.
internal_gateway variable Switches between public and internal exposure with a single line of code. In production, the common setup is an internal LB combined with Application Gateway (WAF).
Inbound traffic for a public Gateway is allowed in the 03-network node NSG A Standard LB blocks inbound traffic by default, and AKS does not add rules to an NSG you attached to the subnet. AllowGatewayHttpHttps in 03-network (80/443, source gateway_allowed_source_prefixes) fills that role, and for an internal Gateway the default rule (AllowVnetInBound) allows traffic from inside the VNet.

Code#

app.tf — the demo app and the essential production resources (PDB, HPA, NetworkPolicy)

gateway.tf — Gateway and HTTPRoute

Walkthrough#

Step 1. Import the app image into ACR#

Step 2. Apply#

Step 3. Verify#

Step 4. Run behavior experiments#

💡Tip

More kubectl practice with pods and Deployments (logs, exec, port-forward, rollouts, troubleshooting) is in Appendix E. This app is managed by Terraform, so do your experiments in a practice namespace: a change made with kubectl shows up as a difference in the next terraform plan (E-8).

Extending to TLS (HTTPS)#

Add a 443/HTTPS listener to the Gateway and point tls.certificateRefs at a Kubernetes Secret. The node NSG (03-network) already allows ports 80 and 443, so you don't need to change the NSG. The Microsoft baseline approach is to keep the certificate in Key Vault and sync it to a Secret with the Secrets Store CSI driver's secretObjects (the same SecretProviderClass pattern as in Lab 06; the Key Vault Certificate User role is required). For the detailed procedure, see App Routing Gateway API: DNS and TLS.

Automated verification script#

It checks Gateway (Programmed) → HTTPRoute (Accepted) → Deployment/HPA/PDB/NetworkPolicy and, for a public Gateway, sends a real curl request and expects 200 (skipped for an internal Gateway).

Common issues#

Symptom Cause / Fix
The ADDRESS of the Gateway is empty The LB is still provisioning (1–3 min). Check the Conditions in kubectl -n web describe gateway web-gateway and kubectl -n web get events. The public IP quota may be exhausted.
Plan error no matches for kind "Gateway" / no GatewayClass azapi_update_resource.gateway_api from Lab 05 was not applied (check whether enable_gateway_api=false was set). Run kubectl get gatewayclass.
ImagePullBackOff az acr import was skipped (image path demo/aspnetapp:v1). Check kubectl describe pod.
curl times out Check that the AllowGatewayHttpHttps rule exists on the 03-network node subnet NSG (AKS does not modify an NSG attached to the subnet, so the rule Terraform creates is required) and that your IP is included in gateway_allowed_source_prefixes. Other causes: you are accessing an internal Gateway (internal_gateway=true) from outside the VNet, or a NetworkPolicy is blocking the traffic.
HTTPRoute shows Accepted: False The parentRefs name does not match, or allowedRoutes (Same namespace) is violated.
