Lab 08

Lab 08. Governance and security: Azure Policy · Defender · locks · budgets#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
30 min (including the wait for policy sync) Free in the default configuration. The Defender plan is billed per vCore (optional) terraform/08-governance 05. AKS cluster

What you build in this lab#

Layer Resource Effect
Cluster configuration checks 6 built-in policies (local account blocking, authorized IP ranges, RBAC, managed identity, Policy add-on, Defender profile) Audit whether the cluster meets best practices
In-cluster (admission) checks Pod security initiatives baseline and restricted Audit or Deny for things like running as non-root, no privilege escalation, and resource limits
Threat detection azurerm_security_center_subscription_pricing (Defender for Containers) Runtime threats, image vulnerabilities, misconfigurations (optional)
Deletion protection azurerm_management_lock Prevents accidental deletion of the network/platform resource groups (optional)
Cost guardrail azurerm_consumption_budget_subscription Monthly budget alerts filtered by the workload tag (optional)

Comparison for AWS engineers#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
SCP (organization permission ceiling) Azure Policy (+ RBAC deny assignments) An SCP is an "IAM permission ceiling"; Azure Policy evaluates resource properties and request content and audits, denies, or modifies.
AWS Config rules / Conformance pack Policy definitions / initiatives (policySet) + compliance state An initiative is the equivalent of a conformance pack. There are a great many built-in definitions.
Kyverno / OPA Gatekeeper Azure Policy for Kubernetes (add-on based on Gatekeeper v3) Assign it with the same azurerm_resource_group_policy_assignment and it is synced to the cluster as Gatekeeper Constraints.
GuardDuty (EKS) / Inspector (ECR) / Security Hub Microsoft Defender for Containers + Defender for Cloud A subscription-level plan + the cluster's microsoft_defender profile.
CloudFormation Termination Protection / SCP deny Resource locks (CanNotDelete / ReadOnly) A lock blocks deletion itself (even for owners). You must remove it before terraform destroy.
AWS Budgets Cost Management budgets Email / action group notifications. Track per workload with a tag filter.

Design decisions (best practices)#

Decision Why
Roll out in phases: Audit → Deny (policy_effect) If you enable Deny from the start, existing workloads get blocked. Review the audit results, sort out the exceptions, and only then raise it to Deny.
Assignment scope = the cluster resource group Keeps the lab scope limited. In production, raise it to a management group or subscription so that every cluster inherits it.
System namespaces in excludedNamespaces Namespaces that AKS manages, such as kube-system, gatekeeper-system, and aks-istio-system, are excluded from evaluation.
The restricted initiative is always Audit It shows "how close you are to the next level (a stricter standard)."
Policy definitions/GUIDs are spelled out in the code Built-in definition IDs are the same worldwide. You can always verify them with az policy definition show --name <GUID>.
Subscription-level Defender plan / locks / budgets are off by default They affect the whole subscription, cost money, or get in the way of deletion, so you turn them on explicitly.
ℹ️Note

In AKS Automatic, many of the policies above are applied by default in enforce mode, through Deployment Safeguards and Pod Security Standards (baseline) → Lab 10.

Code#

policy.tf — Azure Policy assignments

security.tf — Defender plan, resource locks

budget.tf — Budget alerts

Walkthrough#

Step 1. Apply the default (Audit) configuration#

Step 2. Check that the policies synced to the cluster#

The Azure Policy add-on syncs assignments about every 15 minutes. The first sync takes a while.

Expected result: in the default configuration, policies such as authorized-ip-ranges (✓) and local-auth-disabled (✓) show as Compliant, while the Defender profile policy shows as NonCompliant because enable_defender=false → the audit is working as intended.

ℹ️Note

If the subscription already has a Defender for Containers auto-provisioning policy (the default in subscriptions where Defender is on), that policy attaches the Defender profile to the cluster directly, using the subscription's default Defender workspace. In that case the Defender profile policy is Compliant from the start, and the plan for 05-aks keeps showing a diff that removes microsoft_defender. To make Terraform declare the same profile, follow step 4 and reuse the workspace that the profile already uses. Do not point it at the platform workspace from Lab 04: that workspace disables local authentication, which the Defender sensor does not support, and its microsoft-defender-publisher pods crash-loop. The evaluation results also include non-compliant items from subscription-level initiatives (e.g., the ASC default initiative).

Step 3. Try the Deny effect#

ℹ️Note

Create the test pod in the default namespace, not web. The web namespace has Pod Security Standards (baseline enforce) applied, so the same pod is rejected with violates PodSecurity "baseline:latest": privileged before Azure Policy (Gatekeeper) can evaluate it. Both are rejections, but what you want to see in this step is the Azure Policy Deny effect.

When you're done, revert with terraform apply (default Audit). While Deny is on, the apps you deployed in Labs 06 and 07 must also satisfy the policy (the apps in this guide are written to do so).

Step 4. (Optional) Defender / budget / locks#

⚠️Warning

If you clean up while the locks (enable_resource_locks) are still on, terraform destroy fails. Destroy just the lock resources first, before cleaning up: terraform destroy -target=azurerm_management_lock.network -target=azurerm_management_lock.platform (run in this stack). scripts/cleanup.sh does this automatically → Lab 11.

Automated verification script#

It checks the policy assignments and compliance state, the Defender plan, and the resource locks. When the policy effect is the default Audit, non-compliant resources are shown only as a warning (!) (evaluation can take up to tens of minutes right after assignment).

Common issues#

Symptom Cause / Fix
AuthorizationFailed ... policyAssignments/write Missing permission to assign policies (Resource Policy Contributor/Owner).
kubectl get constraints returns nothing The add-on is still syncing (up to 15 min). Check the pod status with kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep azure-policy and kubectl get pods -n gatekeeper-system, and verify that azure_policy_enabled = true.
Compliance state stays at NotStarted The first evaluation is slow (tens of minutes). You can request a manual evaluation with az policy state trigger-scan -g <rg>.
Budget creation error start_date The budget start date must be the first day of the current month (the code computes it automatically with time_static).
Cost goes up after enabling the Defender plan You are billed for the vCores of all AKS nodes in the subscription. Turn it off after the lab with -var enable_defender_plan=false.

Next → Lab 09. Day-2 operations: upgrades · scaling · node replacement · testing

← PreviousLab 07. Ingress: ALB Controller → Gateway API (approuting-istio)Next →Lab 09. Day-2 operations: upgrades · scaling · node replacement · testing
Lab 09

Lab 09. Day-2 operations: upgrades · scaling · node replacement · testing#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
40 min (reading + optional experiments) Extra nodes during experiments No new stack (variable changes in terraform/05-aks) 05. AKS cluster

Operating a cluster safely over time is harder than creating one. This lab explains how to carry out Day-2 tasks as Terraform variable changes, along with the points to watch out for.

Comparison for AWS engineers#

AWS (EKS) Azure (AKS) Differences / notes
Control plane minor upgrade → node group upgrade Auto-upgrade channel or az aks upgrade (control plane first, then node pools) Nodes are replaced in a rolling fashion by adding temporary nodes (up to max_surge). In this lab, Terraform ignores the version after creation (ignore_changes) so that AKS manages it; managing the version in code as well (option C) is covered separately below.
Extended Support (14 months → +12 months, paid) 12 months of support + LTS (Premium tier, optional) From 2027-06, the platform automatically upgrades versions that are out of support (ignoring the maintenance window, and possibly PDBs too → upgrade ahead of time).
Node AMI updates node_os_upgrade_channel (NodeImage) + maintenance_window_node_os Automatically replaces the node image in a weekly window.
Karpenter drift / consolidation NAP (node_provisioning_profile.mode = "Auto") Optional on Standard, default on Automatic. This lab defaults to Cluster Autoscaler (Manual).
Changes through eksctl or the console Change a variable → plan → apply Manual changes (az aks update) cause drift from Terraform, so make changes in code. (Exception: the Kubernetes version is handled with ignore_changes so that AKS manages it.)

1. Upgrade strategy#

Auto-upgrade channels#

Channel Behavior In this lab
none Manual Used in option C (below)
patch Automatically moves to the latest patch of the same minor ✅ Default (you upgrade minor versions yourself after a preflight check)
stable N-1 of the latest GA minor Used by AKS Automatic
rapid Latest GA minor Development environments
node-image Node image only (use node_os_upgrade_channel instead)

When upgrades happen is controlled with maintenance_window_auto_upgrade (Kubernetes version) and maintenance_window_node_os (node OS image). The lab code uses Sunday 02:00 KST / Saturday 02:00 KST, 4 hours.

❗Important

The maintenance window applies only to automatic upgrades. A manual upgrade, where you raise the version with az aks upgrade or Terraform, starts immediately. Run it outside business hours.

Minor upgrades (for example, 1.36 → 1.37, after GA)#

⚠️Warning

As of 2026-10, 1.37 is in preview and is expected to reach GA (automatic upgrades do not move to a preview version). Upgrade production clusters after GA, and in the order development → staging → production. The steps below are an example of the procedure after GA.

❗Important

Why does Terraform "ignore" the Kubernetes version? When AKS automatically upgrades the patch version of a cluster created with a minor alias such as kubernetes_version = "1.36", the actual version (for example, 1.36.6) no longer matches the alias, so in azurerm 5.9.0 and earlier every plan shows a needless diff of 1.36.6 -> 1.36 (#26946). A fix that suppresses this (PR #32625) has been merged and is included in v5.10.0 (scheduled for 2026-10-15). To be safe on any provider version, this lab sets the version only at creation time and afterwards lets AKS manage it with lifecycle { ignore_changes = [kubernetes_version, default_node_pool[0].orchestrator_version] } ([orchestrator_version] for the User/Spot pools). Of the three options below, pick the one that fits your team's operating model.

Option Who upgrades the version Best for In this lab
A. Automatic channel (stable/rapid) AKS, automatically up to the minor version, in the maintenance window Minimal operational burden; dev and small environments (same model as AKS Automatic) Change only the automatic_upgrade_channel value and apply
B. Manual az aks upgrade A person: preflight check first, then control plane → node pools Production clusters where you want patches to be automatic but minor upgrades under your control ✅ Default setup (patch channel + ignore_changes)
C. Terraform as the single source of truth Change the version variable in a PR and apply Organizations that need every change recorded through code review See C-1 / C-2 below

Preflight check (shared by B and C):

B. Manual upgrade (default setup)

Version changes are ignored through ignore_changes, so terraform plan shows no diff. However, when you add a new node pool later (for example, enable_spot_pool = true), the new pool is created with var.kubernetes_version, so align it by passing -var kubernetes_version=<current cluster minor>.

C. Managing the version with Terraform as well (how to switch)

Common to both: remove the kubernetes_version / orchestrator_version entries from lifecycle { ignore_changes } in cluster.tf and in the node pools (user, spot). Then pick one of the two.

  • C-1. Pin the full patch version (works with every provider version): set automatic_upgrade_channel = "none" (keep node_os_upgrade_channel = "NodeImage" for node OS replacement), and set kubernetes_version to a full patch version instead of an alias (for example, 1.36.4). Patch security updates are also applied by hand through variable change → PR → apply.
  • C-2. Keep the alias (requires azurerm ≥ 5.10): keep automatic_upgrade_channel = "patch" and leave the kubernetes_version = "1.36" alias as it is. AKS raises the patch version (the provider treats the alias as equivalent to the actual patch version, which suppresses the diff), and when you raise the alias to "1.37", the minor upgrade shows up in the plan. 5.10.0 has not been released yet, so this guide was verified with 5.9.0. After the release, upgrade with terraform init -upgrade, confirm that plan shows no needless diff, and then use it.

What to watch during the upgrade:

💡Tip

When the upgrade finishes, run scripts/verify.sh 05-aks from the repository root to check, read-only, that all nodes are Ready and the add-on pods are Running. If you changed the upgrade channel (option A / C-1), the changed value is shown as-is.

Checklist Why
PDBs, replicas ≥ 2, readiness probes Availability during drains
Spare subnet IPs (enough for a max_surge of 33%) Temporary nodes consume IPs
Check the list of APIs being removed Manifest/Helm chart compatibility
Add-on/CRD compatibility (the Gateway API bundle is upgraded automatically to match the cluster version) Managed Gateway API CRD v1.5.1 (1.36) → v1.6.1 (1.37+)

2. Scaling#

Layer Tool Setup in this lab
Pod count HPA (CPU/memory), KEDA (event-driven: Service Bus, Kafka …) HPA: Lab 07 / KEDA: workload_autoscaler_profile.keda_enabled
Pod size VPA (recommends requests/limits) vertical_pod_autoscaler_enabled
Node count Cluster Autoscaler (min/max per node pool) system 3–5, user 3–6
Node type NAP (Karpenter) Try it in Lab 10
Cost Spot pool -var enable_spot_pool=true
💡Tip

Don't hard-code the node count. When auto_scaling_enabled = true, declare only min_count/max_count. If you set node_count, it keeps conflicting with the values the autoscaler changes (if you must set it, use lifecycle.ignore_changes).

💡Tip

Scaling a workload by hand (kubectl scale), rolling out a new image, undoing a bad release and reading pod logs are covered in Appendix E. If Terraform owns the workload (Lab 06 and Lab 07), change the code instead of using kubectl, or the next terraform plan shows a difference (E-8).

3. Changing and replacing node pools#

Changing vm_size, os_disk_*, zones, vnet_subnet_id, and similar attributes replaces the node pool. This lab sets temporary_name_for_rotation (systemtmp, usertmp) so that a temporary pool is created first and the replacement happens afterwards. That is why the plan shows will be updated in-place instead of replace; the provider performs the actual replacement (create the temporary pool → remove the old pool) during apply.

🛑Caution

Rotation removes the old pool without cordon/drain, so pods can be interrupted. In production, a blue-green approach (add a new pool → cordon/drain the existing pool → confirm the pods have moved → remove the existing pool) is safer. Even for workloads that have a PDB, always run this during planned maintenance time.

4. Operating habits that save money#

5. Backup and disaster recovery (concepts)#

Need Azure service Notes
Cluster resource / PV backup Azure Backup for AKS (Backup vault + extension) The managed counterpart of Velero. Includes PV snapshots.
Multi-region A cluster per region + Azure Front Door/Traffic Manager; Fleet Manager for multiple clusters The mission-critical pattern from the WAF guide. Design the IP ranges so they don't overlap across regions.
GitOps Flux extension (azurerm_kubernetes_flux_configuration) Bootstrap clusters and deploy apps from Git.

6. Terraform code quality and CI#

This repository provides a three-stage static validation that runs without an Azure subscription.

Stage What it catches
terraform fmt -check Formatting consistency
terraform validate Provider schema violations (for example, arguments removed in azurerm 5.x) — run this first when you upgrade versions
terraform test (mock) Plan logic such as variable validation, count/for_each, conditional expressions, and tag and naming-convention rules

A real PR pipeline adds plan review and security scanning (for example, trivy config, checkov) on top of this. Here is a GitHub Actions (OIDC) example that signs in without passwords (replace the action versions with the latest ones).

ℹ️Note

Drift detection: running terraform plan -detailed-exitcode periodically from a scheduler lets you find settings that someone changed through the portal or CLI (exit code 2).

Lab 10

Lab 10. AKS Automatic: the "we operate it for you" mode, equivalent to EKS Auto Mode#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
30 min (apply 10–15 min) AKS Standard tier + automatically provisioned nodes (delete right after the lab) terraform/10-aks-automatic 02. Remote state (independent of Labs 03–05)
ℹ️Note

As of 2026, Microsoft's Well-Architected guidance recommends the following: "Choose AKS Automatic for most new production workloads, and choose Standard only when you need Windows nodes, LTS, or special network/platform customization." This mode gives you by default what you designed yourself in Lab 05.

What you build in this lab#

What took about 250 lines of cluster.tf plus monitoring and network settings in Lab 05 takes about 20 lines of resources here.

Comparison for AWS engineers#

AWS Azure Differences / notes
EKS Auto Mode AKS Automatic In both, the cloud provider manages the nodes, scaling, upgrades, and main add-ons.
EC2 instances that Auto Mode creates (visible in your account) Managed system node pool hosted in AKS's own subscription The system nodes don't appear in your subscription's VM list.
Karpenter NodePool/EC2NodeClass NAP's NodePool / AKSNodeClass CRDs Same Karpenter-family API.
Configure Pod Security/Kyverno yourself Deployment Safeguards (Azure Policy, enforce) Deployments that violate rules such as resource requests/limits, probes, or the ban on latest tags are rejected.
You can modify EC2 instances directly in the account that manages the nodes Node resource group lock (MC_ can't be modified) Prevents accidentally touching the nodes.

Standard vs. Automatic: which one to choose#

Area AKS Automatic AKS Standard (Lab 05)
System node pool Managed (operated by AKS) You create and operate it
Node scaling NAP only, HPA/KEDA/VPA enabled Choose Cluster Autoscaler or NAP
Tier / SLA Standard + Pod readiness SLA + uptime SLA Free (default) / Standard / Premium (LTS)
Upgrades stable channel (N-1) + automatic node image updates Manual or choose a channel
Authentication Azure RBAC only (no local accounts) Local accounts on by default → turning them off is recommended
Policy Deployment Safeguards + PSS baseline enforce Optional (Lab 08)
Networking Overlay + Cilium, managed NAT, API server VNet Integration Optional (you configure it yourself in Lab 03/05)
Observability Prometheus/Container Insights on by default when created from the portal/CLI → when you create it with Terraform, you connect them yourself You configure it yourself (the DCR pattern from Lab 05)
Constraints No Windows nodes, some extensions unsupported (Dapr, etc.), no conversion from Standard to Automatic Almost none
❗Important

Migrating from Standard to Automatic (in-place conversion) is not supported. Decide up front which one you will use. If it's hard to decide, the recommended order is to start with Automatic and see what falls short.

Design decisions (best practices)#

Decision Why
Default to a managed VNet (use_byo_network = false) Simplest option. If you need to integrate with an existing network or on-premises, you must start with a BYO VNet (it can't be changed afterward).
With BYO: 3 subnets (API server delegated /28, user nodes, system nodes) + UAMI + Network Contributor on the VNet Same requirements as the official Microsoft sample. NAP creates nodes inside the VNet, so it needs permissions at the VNet scope.
ignore_changes = [delegation] on the system node subnet After the cluster is created, AKS adds a delegation to the subnet; this prevents Terraform from trying to revert it.
Ingress: web_app_routing_ingress { istio_enabled = true } Uses the approuting-istio implementation instead of NGINX. Only new Automatic clusters on 1.36+ include the Gateway API CRDs by default (the stable channel is N-1, so clusters are currently created on 1.35 and may not have the CRDs).
api_server_access.authorized_ip_ranges Allow only your own IP on the public endpoint.
Admin permissions: grant_current_user_admin / admin_principal_ids Automatic has no local accounts, so an Azure RBAC role is the only way to get access. In the lab, the role is granted to the signed-in user (default); for teams/CI, turn that off with false and set the Entra group Object ID in admin_principal_ids (if you leave both empty, validation blocks it).

Code#

main.tf — Resource group and (optional) BYO VNet

cluster.tf — The Automatic cluster: compare it with cluster.tf from Lab 05.

Walkthrough#

Step 1. Apply#

ℹ️Note

AKS Automatic turns on Azure Policy automatically. The Microsoft.PolicyInsights resource provider must be registered in the subscription (Lab 01). If the Azure CLI aks-preview extension is installed, it can conflict, so we recommend running az extension remove -n aks-preview.

❗Important

You now have two clusters. az aks get-credentials made this Automatic cluster the current kubectl context, so the commands in the next steps run against it. To go back to the Lab 05 cluster, use kubectl config use-context <name>; kubectl config get-contexts lists both, and az aks list -o table shows their SKUs (Base for Standard, Automatic for this one). See Appendix D. This cluster is not connected to the Lab 04 ACR, so use public images here.

Step 2. Inspect the cluster that has "no" nodes#

💡Tip

To see that address from inside the cluster, run the pod from Appendix D (D-2). A bare kubectl run pod is rejected here because it has no resource requests.

ℹ️Note

A new Automatic cluster is on the stable channel (N-1), so it is created with a version one minor below the latest GA minor (1.35.8 as of 2026-10), and azurerm_kubernetes_automatic_cluster doesn't let you pick the version. In this case istio_enabled = true turns on the approuting-istio implementation, but the Gateway API CRDs aren't installed, so kubectl get gatewayclass fails with the server doesn't have a resource type "gatewayclass" (this is expected). To use Gateway/HTTPRoute, check again after the cluster moves up to 1.36+.

Step 3. Try Deployment Safeguards#

A deployment that doesn't follow the safeguards is rejected (or triggers a warning).

A deployment that follows best practices passes, and its pending pods prompt NAP to create new nodes.

A VM size that fits the pod requirements (CPU/memory) is selected automatically. In Lab 05, this is the part where you chose the node pool's vm_size and min/max yourself.

Step 4. (Optional) Try rebuilding with a BYO VNet#

Step 5. Clean up#

Automated verification script#

It checks the AKS Automatic settings (SKU, NAP, local accounts, upgrade channel) and the nodes/Karpenter NodePool (read-only).

Common issues#

Symptom Cause / Fix
Location is not supported Check that the region supports Automatic (koreacentral, koreasouth, and others are supported).
MissingSubscriptionRegistration ... PolicyInsights az provider register -n Microsoft.PolicyInsights.
Pods stay Pending Not enough vCPU quota (NAP picks the VM family automatically). Check the quota and request an increase; also check kubectl describe pod and kubectl get nodeclaims.
Forbidden (kubectl) Wait for the Azure RBAC role to propagate (up to 5 min). Automatic has no local accounts. If grant_current_user_admin = false, check that you (or a group you belong to) are listed in admin_principal_ids.
LinkedAuthorizationFailed with BYO The UAMI's Network Contributor role is still propagating → retry.

Lab 11

Lab 11. Cleanup: delete everything so costs don't leak#

Duration Estimated cost Terraform stack Prerequisite
20–40 min Billing continues until you clean up All stacks (reverse order) All the labs you completed
🛑Caution

AKS nodes (VMs), NAT Gateway, public IPs, Premium ACR, Managed Grafana, and Defender plans keep billing as long as you leave them on. Always clean up when you finish the labs or before a long break.

The easiest way: the cleanup script#

scripts/cleanup.sh handles everything in one go: deleting in reverse order of creation, removing resource locks, skipping stacks that are already deleted, and checking for leftover resources afterward. First run it with --dry-run to see what it would delete (it deletes nothing).

Safeguard Behavior
Confirmation prompt Without --yes, you must type delete to start. With no input (pipe/CI), the run is canceled.
Subscription check The script doesn't start if ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID differs from the current subscription in az.
Order However you order the stacks you list, the script always sorts them into the safe deletion order (06/07 → 05 → 04 → 03).
Resource locks If the CanNotDelete locks from 08 exist, the script first deletes only the lock resources, using -target. Other 08 settings, such as policy effects, are left alone and deleted later in the proper order.
Re-runs Stacks that are already deleted (empty state) are skipped. If a run fails midway, fix the cause and run the same command again.
Cluster already deleted The Kubernetes resources in 06/07 are removed from state only, and the Azure resources are deleted.
02-bootstrap If the state is still remote, the script doesn't delete it and instead explains how to move it back to local.
ℹ️Note

From Destroy order through Verify the cleanup below, the sections spell out what this script does manually. Use them if you work without the script or want to understand where a run failed.

Destroy order (reverse of creation)#

Delete 06/07 before 05: the kubernetes provider can connect and delete only while the cluster still exists.

Preflight checks (locks and subscription-level settings)#

💡Tip

If you created a lock yourself in the portal or with az lock create, Terraform doesn't know about it. Check with az lock list -o table and delete it with az lock delete -n <lock-name> -g <resource-group>.

Step 1. Destroy each stack#

ℹ️Note

Run this in a terminal where the environment variables (ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, TF_VAR_allowed_ip_ranges, and so on) are set. If you never created 10-aks-automatic, its destroy finishes with "No changes". Before each stack's destroy, get in the habit of checking the deletion list with terraform plan -destroy.

When destroy fails for 06/07 because you deleted the cluster first#

If there is no cluster for the kubernetes provider to connect to, destroy fails. In that case, remove the Kubernetes resources from the state and delete only the Azure resources (the cluster is gone, so the resources inside it are already gone too).

Step 2. Delete the bootstrap (state storage)#

If you moved the 02-bootstrap state to Blob Storage, you can't delete the storage that holds the state itself. First move the state back to local, then delete.

Step 3. Verify the cleanup#

Why the Key Vault is still there#

The Key Vault from Lab 04 has purge_protection_enabled = true (recommended), so even after deletion it holds its name in a soft-deleted state for 7 days. If you recreate it with the same name, the provider recovers it automatically (recover_soft_deleted_key_vaults = true). It incurs no cost. If you want to remove it completely right away, create it with -var key_vault_purge_protection_enabled=false from the start and use az keyvault purge after deleting it.

Emergency cleanup (when Terraform fails)#

Deleting the resource groups outright is the fastest method. It doesn't clean up the state, so use it only when you don't plan to use Terraform again.

Check costs#

  • Portal → Cost Management → Cost analysis → filter: tag lab = aks-terraform-guide (or workload = aksdemo)

  • The day after you delete, confirm that the cost falls to 0 (some items are reflected a day late).

  • If you created a budget (Lab 08), it's deleted during the cleanup.

  • (If you used the cleanup script) Checked the list of resources to delete with --dry-run first

  • Destroyed all stacks

  • The resource group list is empty (lab=aks-terraform-guide)

  • (If you used it) Set the Defender subscription plan back to free

  • Deleted the local .terraform/, backend.hcl, and tfplan files

A-3. Inconsistencies found and fixed during the run#

# Location Symptom Fix
1 05-aks/monitoring.tf The first apply failed with 409 AnotherOperationInProgress: AzAPI's PUT of the cluster overlapped with the creation of the User node pool Added depends_on so that azapi_update_resource.control_plane_metrics runs after the node pool
2 06-workload/kubernetes.tf, 07-ingress/app.tf kv-demo was rejected with violates PodSecurity "restricted": runAsNonRoot != true and failed after waiting 10 minutes for the rollout. The kubernetes provider sends omitted container security_context values as false, which overrides the pod-level true (the app container in 07 had the same configuration) Set run_as_non_root = true explicitly in the container security_context
3 scripts/cleanup.sh With pipefail, tf_state | grep -q had its result flipped by SIGPIPE, so the cluster was judged "already gone" even though it existed, and the Kubernetes resources in 06 were removed from the state. A failure to read the state could also have been mistaken for "empty", causing a stack to be skipped Capture the output in a variable first and treat a read failure as an error
4 scripts/preflight.sh A guest (personal) account cannot look up roles by sign-in name, which produced the warning "Couldn't query roles" Look up roles by the signed-in user's object ID
5 Lab 01 §4 The default subscription quota (e.g., 20 per family · 32 in total) can be lower than the minimum of 24 vCPUs Added a required-capacity table and an az quota create example
6 Lab 03, 03-network comments The explanation that "the Pod CIDR is not part of the VirtualNetwork tag, so the default Deny blocks it" did not match the measurements Corrected: only the public Gateway rule is required; the Pod and API server rules are defensive and needed only when you add a Deny
7 Lab 06 step 1 terraform -chdir=../04-platform fails from the repository root terraform -chdir=terraform/04-platform
8 Lab 06 step 3 base64 -d, used to decode the JWT, truncates the output on macOS because the padding is missing Decode with python after fixing the padding

10 Lab 07 step 3 kubectl logs deploy/… shows only one of the 2 Envoy pods, so you may see just the startup logs Label selector + --prefix
11 Lab 09 §3 The vm_size change plan is shown as updated in-place, not replace (the replacement through a temporary pool happens during apply) Corrected the explanation
12 Lab 10 step 2 Automatic was created at 1.35, so the Gateway API CRD is missing and kubectl get gatewayclass fails Added a note that this applies only to 1.36+
13 Lab 05 · 08 The number of resources stated for the plan did not match reality Lab 05: corrected 16 → 15 (including the resource group); Lab 08: corrected to 8 policy assignments + 1 time_static = 9
14 Lab 08 steps 2 and 4, 05-aks enable_defender With enable_defender=true the Defender profile pointed at the platform workspace, which has local authentication disabled. The Defender sensor does not support that, and its microsoft-defender-publisher pods crash-looped (Local authentication is disabled for the Log Analytics workspace). The earlier runs did not look at those pods Added defender_log_analytics_workspace_id (required with enable_defender) and a test for it, and rewrote the Lab 08 guidance to reuse the workspace that the policy attached

A-4. What could not be verified, and what varies by environment#

  • Spot scale-up (Lab 05 (a)): Adding and removing the pool was verified, but when pods were deployed, no nodes were added because of SkuNotAvailable (Capacity Restrictions: Standard_D4ds_v5). Spot capacity varies by region and time.
  • Upgrade (Lab 09 §1): It could not be run because there was no GA version to upgrade to (1.36.4 is the latest GA, 1.37.0 is in preview, and the node image is also the latest). Rolling replacement (surge · PDB) is unverified.
  • Defender subscription plan (Lab 08 step 4): It was already enabled in this subscription, so it was not run (if Terraform manages it, destroy reverts it to Free, which can change the subscription's existing settings).
  • Subscriptions with a Defender auto-provisioning policy: Right after the cluster is created, it stays in Updating for a while, so the provisioning-state check in verify.sh fails temporarily, and the 05-aks plan keeps showing a diff that removes microsoft_defender. Declaring the same profile (enable_defender=true plus defender_log_analytics_workspace_id set to the workspace that the policy used) makes the diff disappear (Lab 08 steps 2 and 4). Do not use the platform workspace for it (fix 14 in A-3).
  • Subscriptions where an organization policy turns off public access to Storage: In a subscription where an Azure Policy (Modify) at the management group changes a storage account's public network access to Disabled, remote state access in Lab 02 failed with 403 AuthorizationFailure (even if Terraform creates the account with Enabled, the policy changes it). This guide assumes a public endpoint + Entra authentication, so you need a policy exemption or a different subscription.
  • terraform plan -detailed-exitcode: It returns 2 even when the provider changes only the available_kubernetes_versions output value (no actual infrastructure change). Ignore this value when your CI decides whether there are "no changes".
  • Not run: Windows (PowerShell) commands, other regions, team environments (Entra group admin_principal_ids), an actual deployment with enable_private_cluster=true (plan only), a TLS (443) listener, Application Gateway for Containers, signing in to the Grafana web UI, interactive sign-in with az login, and the GitHub Actions workflow example in Lab 09 §6.
  • Intermittent Azure CLI error: az aks get-credentials failed once with Error loading command module 'serviceconnector': deadlock and succeeded when run again (a problem on the CLI side).

B. Troubleshooting collection#

Symptom Cause / fix
Error: ... subscription_id is a required provider property Set the ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID environment variable (Lab 01).
MissingSubscriptionRegistration / ResourceProviderNotRegistered Register the RP (azurerm 5.x does not register providers automatically). az provider register --namespace Microsoft.XXX.
AuthorizationFailed The current user lacks permissions (Contributor + User Access Administrator, or Owner), or a role assignment you just created is still propagating (up to 5 min).
Error acquiring the state lock Another run is in progress, or a previous run exited abnormally. Use terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> only when you are sure.
Error: Unsupported argument / Missing required argument (azurerm) Differences between 4.x code and the 5.x schema. Locate the problem with terraform validate and see the 5.0 upgrade guide.
Provider produced inconsistent result after apply (kubernetes_manifest) CRD defaults / server-side normalization differences. Retry terraform apply or use computed_fields.
StorageAccountAlreadyTaken / VaultAlreadyExists / ACR name conflict Globally unique name conflict. Change TF_VAR_workload, or recover/purge the soft-deleted Key Vault.
terraform destroy fails with ScopeLocked Remove the resource lock (Lab 08, Lab 11).
kubectl: Unable to connect ... i/o timeout The API server only accepts the IPs in allowed_ip_ranges. Your public IP changed, or you are on another network, Cloud Shell or CI → see section D (D-3 and D-4): update TF_VAR_allowed_ip_ranges and apply 04-platform, 05-aks and 10-aks-automatic; meanwhile use az aks command invoke.
kubectl changes the wrong cluster With two clusters, az aks get-credentials switches the current context to the cluster you fetched last. Check kubectl config current-context, then kubectl config use-context <name> (see D-1).
kubelogin error / Unauthorized Rerun az login, run kubelogin convert-kubeconfig -l azurecli, and wait for the Azure RBAC role to propagate.
terraform plan asks for a node_count change every time Conflict with the autoscaler. Don't set node_count in the code; use only min_count/max_count (Lab 09).
409 ... AnotherOperationInProgress (azapi_update_resource) It overlapped with another operation on the same cluster (such as node pool creation). The code in this guide fixes the order with depends_on; if they still overlapped, rerun terraform apply after the other operation finishes.
kubernetes_deployment_v1 fails after 10 minutes with Waiting for rollout to finish This happens when the pods are not being created. Check the FailedCreate reason in kubectl -n <namespace> get events (e.g., violates PodSecurity "restricted" → run_as_non_root in the container security_context).
terraform init -migrate-state fails with 403 AuthorizationFailure If the role assignment you just created is still propagating, retry after 1–5 minutes. If it persists, check az storage account show -n <account> --query publicNetworkAccess. If it is Disabled, an organization policy has turned off public access, so you need a policy exemption or a different subscription.

C. Checklist before going to production#

This guide is a cost-balanced setup for learning and PoCs. For production, use the Microsoft AKS baseline architecture as your reference and add the following.

Area This guide Production recommendation
Network topology Single VNet + NAT Gateway Hub-and-spoke: Azure Firewall (egress control, UDR) · Bastion · VPN/ExpressRoute in the hub, AKS in the spoke
API server Public + authorized IP Fully private (enable_private_cluster) + Bastion / jump host / self-hosted runner
Ingress Gateway API public LB Application Gateway (WAF v2) or Front Door → internal Gateway, TLS termination (Key Vault certificate)
Registry / KV Private Endpoint + admin IP allowed Public access fully blocked, CI on in-VNet / managed runners
Identity Roles assigned directly to users Entra groups + PIM (just-in-time), Conditional Access, access reviews
Governance Policy at RG scope (Audit) Policies / initiatives at management group scope + Deny, tag inheritance and required-tag policies
Security Optional Defender Defender for Containers + (Sentinel connector), image signing / scanning pipeline
Resilience Single region (3 zones) Azure Backup for AKS, multi-region + Front Door / Traffic Manager, Fleet Manager
Deployment terraform apply + kubectl GitOps (Flux extension) for cluster bootstrapping / app deployment, OIDC sign-in from pipelines
Modularization Defined directly, for learning Standardize on in-house modules or Azure Verified Modules (AVM)
Observability Default dashboards Prometheus alert rules (azurerm_monitor_alert_prometheus_rule_group) + Action Group, SLO dashboards

D. How to reach the clusters, and what is exposed to the internet#

After Lab 05 and Lab 10 you have two clusters in the same subscription. This section shows how to tell them apart, which traffic can enter and leave, and what to do when you are not on the laptop you used for the labs (Azure Cloud Shell, another PC, CI).

D-1. The two clusters#

Standard (Lab 05) Automatic (Lab 10)
Terraform stack terraform/05-aks (builds on the network and platform stacks 03 and 04) terraform/10-aks-automatic (independent of Lab 03–05)
Default name aks-aksdemo-dev-krc in rg-aksdemo-dev-krc-aks aksa-aksdemo-dev-krc in rg-aksdemo-dev-krc-automatic
SKU in az aks list Base (tier Standard) Automatic (tier Standard)
Nodes System and user pools that you size (default 3 + 3) A managed system pool, plus nodes that node auto-provisioning (NAP) adds on demand
kubectl context Same as the cluster name Same as the cluster name

The names depend on TF_VAR_workload, TF_VAR_environment and TF_VAR_location; read the exact values from the cluster_name and resource_group_name outputs of each stack.

⚠️Warning

az aks get-credentials makes the cluster you fetched last the current context. After Lab 10 step 1, every plain kubectl command goes to the Automatic cluster until you run kubectl config use-context again. Check kubectl config current-context before any apply or delete. The scripts/verify.sh scripts are not affected because they use a temporary kubeconfig.

D-2. What can connect to what#

Standard cluster Automatic cluster
Outbound (cluster → internet) Yes, through the NAT Gateway from Lab 03 (static public IP, nat_gateway_public_ip output) Yes, through the NAT Gateway that AKS manages in the node resource group (MC_…)
API server Public endpoint with API Server VNet Integration. Only the IPs in allowed_ip_ranges can use it Same
Apps reachable from the internet The Lab 07 Gateway has a public IP on ports 80 and 443 (node NSG rule AllowGatewayHttpHttps); internal_gateway=true makes it private None: the guide deploys no LoadBalancer Service here
Images from the Lab 04 ACR Pulled over the Private Endpoint; only this cluster's kubelet identity has AcrPull Cannot pull (ErrImagePull … 403 Forbidden). Use public images such as mcr.microsoft.com, or give your own registry AcrPull and network access

The platform services from Lab 04 do not belong to one cluster: the ACR and Key Vault public endpoints accept only the IPs in allowed_ip_ranges, and Grafana has a public endpoint behind Entra ID sign-in.

Check the outbound IP from inside a cluster. The pod below also follows the Automatic cluster's Deployment Safeguards (resource requests are mandatory there), so the same manifest works on both clusters.

D-3. Where can I run kubectl from?#

From kubectl to the API servers Why
The laptop whose IP is in allowed_ip_ranges Works The IP is authorized
Another network (other Wi-Fi, VPN, tethering) or a teammate's PC Blocked The IP is not authorized
Azure Cloud Shell Blocked Cloud Shell runs on Microsoft-managed Azure addresses that are not in your list, and a fixed address is not guaranteed
CI runners (for example GitHub-hosted runners) Blocked Same reason
Anywhere, with az aks command invoke or the portal Run command Works The command runs inside the cluster through the Azure API, not over your network path

A blocked request gets no answer at all, so kubectl ends with Unable to connect to the server: dial tcp …:443: i/o timeout. (Measured for this guide: from an unauthorized address the TCP connection opens but the HTTPS request gets no response, while the same request from an authorized address returns HTTP 401, which means it reached the API server.)

az aks command invoke runs a command in the cluster through the Azure API, so it works from anywhere you are signed in to Azure:

  • You need Azure RBAC permission on the cluster for the actions Microsoft.ContainerService/managedClusters/runcommand/action and Microsoft.ContainerService/managedClusters/commandResults/read (Owner, Contributor and the AKS Contributor role have them).
  • AKS runs the command in a short-lived pod in the aks-command namespace and returns the text output. There is no interactive shell, exec -it or port-forward; keep each call to commands that finish on their own, and attach files such as a manifest with --file.
  • The portal offers the same feature as AKS cluster → Run command.
  • Tested on both clusters of this guide.

D-4. When your public IP changes, or a teammate needs access#

  1. Look up the new address (Lab 01, step 5): curl -s https://api.ipify.org.
  2. Put every machine that needs access into TF_VAR_allowed_ip_ranges (a JSON list with one /32 per machine) and save it in your env.sh, for example export TF_VAR_allowed_ip_ranges='["203.0.113.10/32","198.51.100.7/32"]'.
  3. Re-apply the three stacks that use the list:
Stack What the IP list opens Command (from the repository root)
04-platform ACR and Key Vault firewalls (needed for az acr import and Key Vault secrets) terraform -chdir=terraform/04-platform apply
05-aks Standard cluster API server terraform -chdir=terraform/05-aks apply
10-aks-automatic Automatic cluster API server terraform -chdir=terraform/10-aks-automatic apply

These applies talk to Azure Resource Manager only, so they work even while kubectl is blocked. A new list takes up to two minutes to propagate. Until then, use az aks command invoke.

⚠️Warning

Do not run the Lab 01 one-liner (curl … api.ipify.org) inside Cloud Shell to fill TF_VAR_allowed_ip_ranges: it would register Cloud Shell's address instead of your laptop's. Run Terraform from your own machine, and use az aks command invoke from Cloud Shell. From an unauthorized address, the kubectl steps of scripts/verify.sh and the stacks that use the kubernetes provider (06 and 07) cannot reach the API server either.

E. Handling Kubernetes workloads with kubectl#

Labs 01–10 build the platform. This section is about the Kubernetes objects that run on it: how to look at them, change them and debug them, and how that fits with Terraform and Azure RBAC. Every command here was run against a cluster from this guide in a throwaway namespace; they work on both clusters unless noted.

E-1. Pick the cluster and namespace#

E-2. Create a practice namespace and a first Deployment#

Practice in a namespace of your own so that you never touch the Lab 06 and Lab 07 apps (demo, web).

The manifest follows the same rules as the Lab 07 app, so it passes on both clusters:

  • resources.requests and limits: on the Automatic cluster (Lab 10), Deployment Safeguards reject a bare pod without requests, and add default values (with a warning) to a Deployment that has none. The scheduler needs them everywhere.
  • Probes: the readiness probe decides when a pod receives traffic, and the liveness probe restarts a stuck container. Deployment Safeguards warn when they are missing.
  • runAsNonRoot, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, drop: ["ALL"] and seccompProfile: the Pod Security rules and the Lab 08 policies.
  • The image is a public sample so that it also runs on the Automatic cluster (see the ACR row in D-2).

E-3. Look at things (read-only)#

E-4. Get inside a pod#

  • exec, logs, cp and port-forward go through the API server, so they work only from where kubectl works (see D-3).
  • A debug container stays in the pod's spec until the pod is replaced.
  • On the Automatic cluster, kubectl run cannot set resource requests, so the throw-away pod is rejected. Use a manifest with requests, as in D-2.

E-5. Change things#

A rolling update protects you from a bad release. Try kubectl -n practice set image deploy/hello hello=mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/samples:does-not-exist: only the new pod goes to ImagePullBackOff, the old pods keep serving, rollout status eventually fails with timed out waiting for the condition, and kubectl -n practice rollout undo deploy/hello restores the working revision. With an autoscaler (HPA) the HPA owns the replica count, so a manual kubectl scale is overridden.

E-6. Configuration data and batch jobs#

⚠️Warning

A Kubernetes Secret is only base64-encoded, not encrypted: kubectl get secret db -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' prints a value that anyone with read access can decode. Do not commit Secret manifests, and keep real secrets out of your shell history. For real applications read secrets from Key Vault (Lab 06).

E-7. When something is wrong: a triage playbook#

Start with these three commands, then use the table.

Symptom Where to look Usual cause and fix
Pending describe pod → Events, for example 0/6 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint(s) The requests are larger than any node can offer, or only tainted nodes are left (the system pool accepts critical add-ons only). Lower the requests; if nodes cannot be added, check the vCPU quota (Lab 01 step 4)
ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull The event message of describe pod A typo in the image or tag; the image was not imported into the ACR (Lab 04, Lab 06); the cluster has no AcrPull or is blocked by the registry firewall (403 Forbidden, see D-2)
CrashLoopBackOff / Error kubectl logs <pod>, --previous, describe → Last State and Exit Code The application exits: a wrong command, environment variable or config; a failing liveness probe; a missing ConfigMap or Secret (CreateContainerConfigError). --previous can be unavailable for a container that restarts very fast, so read the current logs as well
OOMKilled (exit code 137) describe pod → Last State The memory limit is lower than what the process needs. Raise limits.memory or fix the leak; compare with kubectl top pod
The pod disappeared, or Evicted get events Node pressure, or node consolidation (NAP on the Automatic cluster evicts under-used nodes). A bare pod with no owner is not recreated, so run workloads through a Deployment or Job
Forbidden on create or apply The message names the rule denied the request from Gatekeeper or Deployment Safeguards (Lab 08, Lab 10), violates PodSecurity, or an RBAC error (kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n practice)
A Service returns nothing kubectl -n practice get endpoints hello No endpoints: the selector does not match the pod labels (get pods --show-labels), or the readiness probe fails
Unable to connect … i/o timeout Your public IP The IP is not authorized: see D-3 and D-4
You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized) Your sign-in Run az login and kubelogin convert-kubeconfig -l azurecli again

Try it: a pod that exits at once (command: ["sh","-c","echo boom; exit 1"]) shows Error and then CrashLoopBackOff, and its output is in kubectl logs. A pod that asks for cpu: "64" stays Pending with the scheduler event above.

E-8. Terraform-managed or kubectl-managed?#

The Lab 06 and Lab 07 workloads (kv-demo, aspnetapp, the Gateway) belong to Terraform. If you change a field that Terraform manages with kubectl, the next terraform plan shows a difference and the next apply reverts your change:

Rules of thumb:

  1. Experiments belong in your own namespace and are done with kubectl (this section).
  2. Permanent changes to the Lab 06 and Lab 07 workloads are made in the Terraform code or its variables, then applied.
  3. Fields that a controller owns are excluded on purpose: the replica count of the Lab 07 Deployment is ignore_changes because the HPA manages it, so scaling it by hand does not show up as a difference.
  4. To find manual changes, run terraform plan -detailed-exitcode regularly (Lab 09).

E-9. Who may do what: Azure RBAC for Kubernetes#

Local accounts are disabled, so permissions come from Azure roles (Lab 05):

Role Scope What it allows
Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Reader Cluster or namespace Read most objects
Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Writer Cluster or namespace Read and write most objects
Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Admin Cluster or namespace Read and write most objects, and manage roles and role bindings in the namespace
Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin Cluster Everything in every namespace (the lab gives this to the signed-in user)

To give an application team access to one namespace only, assign the role at namespace scope. They also need the Azure Kubernetes Service Cluster User Role on the cluster (to run az aks get-credentials) and their IP in allowed_ip_ranges (D-4):

kubectl auth can-i --list is incomplete on a cluster that uses Azure RBAC (it warns that the webhook authorizer does not support rule resolution), so check one permission at a time. In a team, prefer Entra groups over individual users.

E-10. Clean up the practice namespace#

This does not touch the Lab 06 and Lab 07 workloads or any Azure resource.

I. Verification and cleanup scripts#

The check and delete commands you type by hand during the labs are bundled into scripts. They all live in scripts/ at the repository root and run on macOS · Linux · WSL · Azure Cloud Shell (bash) (requires terraform, az, jq, and, from 05 onward, kubectl and kubelogin).

Script When What it does Source included in
scripts/preflight.sh Lab 01, before you start the labs Checks tools · sign-in · environment variables · Resource Providers · vCPU quota · VM size · permissions (read-only) Lab 01
scripts/verify.sh [stack…] Right after you apply each stack Finds names with terraform output and verifies the results with az/kubectl; prints a ✓ ✗ ! - summary and an exit code (read-only) This appendix
scripts/verify/02…10.sh Called by the script above (can also be run directly) Per-stack verification items 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 10
scripts/cleanup.sh Lab 11, after you finish the labs destroy in reverse order of creation, resource lock removal, safe to re-run, check for leftover resources (supports --dry-run) Lab 11
scripts/lib/common.sh The scripts above source it Result output (pass/fail/warn), value comparison (expect_*), JSON helpers (jq), terraform output/az/kubectl wrappers This appendix
tools/validate-all.sh After you change the code fmt · validate · terraform test (no subscription needed) + script syntax checks F above
💡Tip

The verification scripts are read-only (apart from running printenv/test -s inside a pod, they change nothing). kubectl uses a temporary kubeconfig, so ~/.kube/config is not modified. If you set an option that you can choose with a variable (sku_tier, enable_private_cluster, enable_gateway_api, nat_gateway_sku, etc.) to something other than its default, the scripts show the value or mark it as a warning (!) or skipped (-) instead of reporting a failure (✗). To add verification for a new stack, create a verify_stack function in scripts/verify/NN-name.sh and add the name to ALL_STACKS in verify.sh.

scripts/lib/common.sh — common functions for all scripts

scripts/verify.sh — entry point that calls the per-stack verification scripts

.shellcheckrc — ShellCheck configuration (resolves source paths relative to the script location)
